body: Somewhere in the night it rained, and he never heard it. The window over Theo’s desk is beaded top to bottom, and the eucalyptus in the courtyard is letting the night go a leaf at a time, a drop and then another onto the sill. Past the tree the sky over the Grove is weak tea, thin and brownish, clearing at the edges toward the hills. Down the hall somebody is in the shower with a radio, singing half a beat behind it.

He has been up off the step since twenty past six. Not to sleep. He has stood under the shower in the fourth-floor bathroom till the hot gave out, and gone over his fingers with the bar of Dial somebody abandoned on the ledge in September, because at four in the morning he ate a sleeve of orange crackers out of a vending machine, every one, and the orange was still on him. He has a clean shirt on, the blue oxford from the bottom of the drawer. Not the flannel. She has the flannel, on Del Playa.

His eyes feel sanded. His face has the stiff, rinsed feel it gets after a night like that one, as if it had been taken off and put back on a quarter inch wrong. Over his own bed the crucifix has the window’s light on it. He says the Morning Offering to it while he does the buttons, the short one Ma taught him at the kitchen table, fast, the way you say a thing you have said every morning of your life, and at the end, without planning to, he adds *and her*, and doesn’t say which, and leaves God to sort it out.

Theo is asleep on top of his covers in the blazer again, on his back, one arm off the side of the bed with the knuckles resting on the carpet, the tie rolled in the breast pocket and one good shoe still on. He came up the three steps to four at first light and went down like a building, all at once and straight down, and hasn’t moved since.

Jack crouches at the foot of Theo’s bed and works the knot out of the one shoe, a brown wingtip with the lace pulled tight by a man who meant to walk somewhere in it, and eases it off and sets it beside its mate on the carpet, toes to the wall. Theo doesn’t stir. There’s a hole in the heel of his sock. Jack leaves him the blazer. You don’t get a blazer off a sleeping man without waking him, and Theo has earned the blazer.
Six thirty-eight came and went while he was under the water.

The RAZR is on his desk, shut, where he left it. He picks it up and the little outside screen comes on in his palm: the time, the bars, the battery. Nothing else. For three months of mornings the first thing on that screen has been lowercase. A line about the fog on Del Playa, or a dream she’d had and wanted a ruling on, or the goose; on a bad morning, just *morning*. He catches himself, with the phone in his palm, listening for it anyway. Down the hall the shower shuts off.

body.text: Inside, under the hinge, the last thing that came is still the last thing on it.
body.else: Inside, under the hinge, the last thing on it is the line he sent from the guardrail, with nothing under it.

body: He doesn’t open the other thread. He doesn’t delete anything out of it, either.

The want, this far into Lent, is smaller than it was. It’s the hands that have got worse. They want something to do. They want the hinge of the phone, open and shut and open; they want a lighter that isn’t there, the wheel under the thumb, the scratch and catch of it; left alone, they go looking on their own. His right hand goes to the breast pocket of the Carhartt and finds the pack where it went back at first light, out of Theo’s blazer: the cellophane, the seal, the corners gone soft from the pocket. He leaves it there and brings the hand away.

body.text: *I’ll be here.* She typed it at sixteen minutes past seven last night, and he has had the whole night to work out what she meant by *here*. Here is two floors down.
body.else: *I’ll find you tomorrow.* He typed it on a guardrail with his thumbs not working, and it’s tomorrow, and she’s two floors down.

choices.text: *Read her line again.*

response.text: He opens it. *I’ll be here.* A full stop, a dash, her initial. He reads it for the shape, the way he learned the Baltimore Catechism at seven, off index cards at the kitchen table on Glenwood, so the answers would be there later without his having to go and look.
response.else: He opens it and reads his own line, and the empty space under it, for the shape, the way he learned the Baltimore Catechism at seven, off index cards at the kitchen table on Glenwood, so the answers would be there later without his having to go and look.

response: He sits down on the edge of his bed and laces his boots, double knots, both of them, and doesn’t hurry the second one. Two floors. He would like to arrive with something besides his heart in his mouth.

choices.text: *Put the phone away without opening it.*
response: Into the breast pocket, on top of the pack, the hinge against the cellophane. Whatever is coming at him today isn’t coming on that screen, and he has somewhere to be.
Across the room Theo says, crisp as a clapperboard, in his sleep: “Cut.” He turns over to face the wall.

choices.text: *Check that the ringer’s on. Twice.*
response: It’s on. It has been on since August, Mass excepted. He checks it again anyway, thumbing down through the menu to the little bell and back out to the screen with nothing new on it. The little bell is there. The bars are there. He stands in the middle of 412 in a clean shirt and holds the phone up to the window, to the weak light, and shuts it.

s02.slug: WEDNESDAY · 8:05 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — HERE
body: The stairwell door on four lets him through with its usual complaint, and the well is full of morning. The tube over the landing has gone thin and useless against the daylight. Down at the turn the wired glass is still beaded from the night, and the light through it lays the shadow of the chicken wire across the cinderblock in a slanted grid that shivers whenever a drop lets go.

body.text: He passes his own step, the third one down. On Sunday night he sat on it and nodded to her, and said nothing.
He passes his own step, the third one down. On Sunday night he gave her *Tuesday* from it, and nothing else.
He passes his own step, the third one down. On Sunday night he told her from it that he was sorry it hurt him.
He passes his own step, the third one down.

body: He goes down. The rail is cold and a little wet under his hand where the glass has been sweating onto it. Past the door on three, past the landing, round the turn onto the flight that goes down toward two, and he takes it a step at a time. He has taken these stairs three at a time since August.

Halfway down it comes to him that *here* could mean anything. Here, Marisol. Here, the Commons at the window table. Here, St. Brendan’s at the twelve-ten, in the pew she likes on the Mary side. Here, in general, on the earth, alive: a thing a person might say to a man who sent her a text like that from a guardrail. He had it worked out at four in the morning. He comes round the last turn with his hand on the rail and his heart going like he ran the flights instead of walking them.

She’s on her landing. She’s sitting sideways on the step where she takes her calls, three up from the landing, with her back against the cinderblock and her knees drawn up, so that she can see up the flight and down it at once. She’s dressed for class: jeans, the brown boots, her bag against the wall with a library spine showing at the flap, and the long dark coat, open this morning all the way down. At her collarbone, where he can see it, Grandmère Lucille’s medal lies on its chain against her shirt. On the step below her boots are two Commons coffees in brown paper sleeves gone soft at the seams. One has a tan ring at the sip hole where the milk has come up through it. The other doesn’t.

The step is hers. She has sat on it since September to call home, and he has heard her on it from two floors up on other nights, arguing with a sister about a christening, telling her mother the weather.

The morning goes past before either of them says a word. Rafi Ochoa comes down from three in a towel and shower shoes with a caddy on his hip, trailing Axe and steam, on his way home to two, whose hot water has been out since Monday. He edges past Jack on the rail side and past her on the wall side with a nod for each of them, a man with no dignity left to lose, and the door on two takes him. Then the well is empty, and the glass on the landing drips.

body.text: “You found me,” Lena says.
body.else: “You said you’d find me,” Lena says.

body.text: “I said I would.”

body: She looks at him from the step: the wet hair, the oxford, whatever his face has been doing since six. Her eyes go to the oxford and come back up, and she lets it go by.
“Youngstown,” she says.
She says it like a door held open. He doesn’t answer it, because anything he said would be too much.

He has had this face across a table, across an argument, across a levee in the dark, and since the levee across a rule. This morning she’s pale under the freckles, and there’s a freckle just under her ear he has been not looking at since September. Her hair is pinned up off her neck any old way, for speed, and one piece of it has already given up and come down against her cheek. There’s a crease on her cheek from a pillow, or a sleeve. She looks like somebody who got up early to be somewhere. He would like, more than he has wanted most things in his life, to sit down on that step beside her. There’s room. There is about one coat’s width of room. He stays three steps up, with his hands hanging, and his knees ache from the night.
“You look like you didn’t sleep.”
“I didn’t.”

She nods, unsurprised. She hasn’t handed him anything yet. The black coffee stays on the step by her boot, and both her hands stay around her own cup, and she looks up at him straight and asks it first, before anything else.
“Is she all right?”
“No.”
She takes that. Her face doesn’t do anything with it; she looks past him, up the flight, at nothing in particular, for about the length of a Glory Be, and comes back.
“Is somebody with her?”
“Sol. Theo went.”
It’s the first time anybody has asked him, and it comes out of him that small.

“Good.” She looks down at the lid of her cup, and nods again, slowly, like somebody putting a thing on a high shelf where it will keep. She asks nothing about what was said. He would have had no idea where to start.

She picks up the black one and holds it up to him. He comes down the last few steps and takes it, and that’s where his hands give him away. They haven’t been steady since the guardrail: a night with no sleep in them, and Lent, and nowhere to go. The cup shakes enough to slop coffee up through the sip hole and over the lid. She sees it. She reaches up and takes the lid by its rim, and her other hand comes round over the back of his on the cup, to hold it still while she works the lid loose. Her fingers are cold from the concrete. They stay on the back of his hand while the lid comes free, and a little after it’s free, two seconds, about, long enough for him to feel the hard small ridge on her middle finger where the pen rides, and then the lid is on her knee and her hand is back around her own cup.
He can feel where her fingers were. Not warmth; they were cold. The places themselves, a small cold map across the back of his hand that takes its time going.
He stands on her stairs with the steam coming up into his face and holds the coffee, much too hot to drink.
“It’s Commons coffee,” she says. “It has sat on this step long enough to go bad and not long enough to go cold, and I make no claims for it.”
“It’s good.”
“It is not good. It is hot, and it is here.” She looks at her watch. It tells her what she knew. “The Stations are at seven on Friday. I’ll be at them.”
“I know.”
“I know you know.”
She looks at him a moment more, at the oxford and the eyes over it. “Sleep today. Skip something.”
“I’ve got two classes.”
“Skip one of them. God will understand. Your professor won’t, but God will, and you can take it up with your professor in purgatory.”
Her eight o’clock started ten minutes ago. The strap of her bag is already over her arm. There is one thing he came down to say. It isn’t right yet. He is going to say it anyway.

choices.text: “I’m not going to ask you anything today. Not the day after.”
choices.key: On the stairs the morning after, you told Lena you wouldn’t ask her anything that day — not the day after.
response: “I know.” She keeps her eyes on him over the rim of her cup, and doesn’t make him wait for the rest. “That’s how I know it’s you.”

She gets up, and for the length of a step they’re level, close enough that he gets the cold off her coat and the coffee and under it her soap, and she doesn’t touch him and he doesn’t touch her, and the not-touching has her whole face in it. Then she has the bag on her shoulder and her own cup in her hand, and she goes on down the flight toward two, quick, one hand skimming the rail, and he listens to her boots take the turn below him and go.
The black one is the one she brought him. It’s still too hot. He holds it anyway, in both hands, on her stairs.

choices.text: “I’m going to ask you something. Not today.”
choices.key: On the stairs the morning after, you told Lena you were going to ask her something — just not that day.
response: “I know you are.” She looks up at him with her head a little on one side, as if she might take it up later, and puts it away. “Not today, then.” She sets the lid down on the step beside her, very precisely, like a card she means to come back for.
She stands with her bag and her cup and goes on down toward two, her boots quick on the concrete, and at the turn of the stair, without looking back, she says, “Drink that.”

choices.text: “You said *here*. I’m from Youngstown. We take things literally.”
choices.key: On the stairs the morning after, you told Lena that in Youngstown you take things literally.
response: “So do I.” She tips her own cup at the one in his hands. “I brought two.”
She studies him over the lid. “You’re not going to ask me anything today.”
“No.”

“I’d have worried if you did. I’d have had to send you back up those stairs to bed, and you’d have gone, and then where would we be.” She stands and swings the bag up and goes down past the landing toward the ground, and far below, the door at the foot of the well lets her out into the morning.
When she’s gone he sits down on her step. The concrete is warm where she was.

choices.text: *Sit down two steps below her. Drink the coffee.*
choices.key: On the stairs the morning after, you sat two steps below Lena with the coffee she’d brought and didn’t ask her anything.
response: He comes down past her and sits two steps below, with his back to the wall and the cup in both hands. It’s black and burnt at the bottom, Commons coffee all the way down, and he’d drink a gallon of it.
She lets the quiet run. The tube hums. The beaded glass on the landing goes bright a drop at a time. When she speaks, it’s to the top of his head. “You’re not going to ask me anything today.”
He shakes his head. He doesn’t trust anything else he has.

“Good,” Lena says. “Then I can go be late for my eight o’clock with a clear conscience.” She stands, and comes down past him on the rail side with her coat held in close so it doesn’t brush him, and goes on to the ground with her boots loud in the empty well.
He drinks it too hot and doesn’t care.

s03.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — A LITTLE BROKEN HEART
body: Two classes behind him, and he could not pass a quiz on either. He’s back at his desk in 412 with *The Moviegoer* open for Thursday at a page he has been on since he sat down, and the window has dried, and the eucalyptus has stopped dripping and gone back to smelling like a cough drop and a cat.

Theo is awake, more or less. He has traded the blazer for an old navy cashmere sweater with a hole at one elbow, and he’s lying on top of the covers again with his ankles crossed and his iPhone on his chest. A screenplay lies splayed on the carpet where it slid off the bed.
Theo is thumbing down his News Feed. His thumb stops, and stays stopped. Then he lays the iPhone face down on his chest and goes on looking at the ceiling.
A minute later the RAZR goes off by Jack’s elbow, and keeps going.

body: In Theo’s News Feed it sits between somebody’s album from a formal and a quiz about which *Lost* character you are, and beside it there’s a little broken heart. Jack thumbs over to his own page. His name; his school; his town; the picture from orientation he has never bothered to change. The line that used to be under his name is gone.

It went up in January under the canopy of a gas station in Buellton, at island four, with the pump ticking in the tank. She typed his name into her own phone with her thumb and pressed it, and read the request over his arm when it came up, and said, *That’s the first thing anybody’s ever watched me do that nobody wrote.* He walked off to the air hose in the dark and called his mother first, and came back and pressed Confirm, and a trucker at the diesel island leaned on his horn.

He didn’t touch it today. He hasn’t been on Facebook since Sunday. He doesn’t have to ask whose hand it was. Somebody sat down at twelve minutes past three on a Wednesday afternoon and did the public part herself, without a word to him, and let the site do the rest. It’s the only thing she has sent him since the porch. It’s addressed to everybody else.
He hands the phone back. Theo takes it and sets it on his chest again, and the radiator ticks, and of all the things Theo could say about her, he says none of them.
He has her side of it. He’s had it since Tuesday night, and it has been in this room all day on the other bed.

choices.text: “Good. She should be the one.”
response: Theo looks at him across the room for a long second, as if a line in a script had come out better than he expected. “Okay.”
He turns the phone over again, screen to the sweater, and reaches down to the carpet for the screenplay, and holds it open over his face.

response: He doesn’t answer the last one. He leaves it lit on the desk, and gets up off the chair and takes his jacket down off the hook, and if Gina could see his face she would make fun of it till Easter.

choices.text: *Close the phone. Look at the ceiling.*
response: He lies back on his own bed and looks up. The water stain over the door, Lake Erie with a bite out of it. The radiator. Theo breathing, slow, across the room. The square of sun from the window working its way up the wall toward the crucifix.
Eventually Theo says, “Commons. You. Food.”
Jack sits up. “You coming?”
Theo doesn’t move. Jack gets his jacket and goes, and Theo doesn’t come. One of them needs to lie there a while longer, and it’s Theo.

s04.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — THE SECOND FLOOR
body: Somebody on two has a door open and a song going, the one every other door on two has been playing since January, loud enough to come through the wired glass of the stairwell door and meet him on the way down. He passes her step on the way. The lid of his coffee is still on it, where she must have set it down when she stood, a white plastic Commons lid with a brown bead dried in the sip hole. He picks it up and puts it in his pocket. He’s on the last flight to the second-floor landing, hands in the Carhartt’s pockets and the Commons somewhere in his future, when the hall beyond the glass fills up with Laney Price.

She is coming down the second-floor hall from the far end at the speed-walk of a woman with news, in socks, on industrial carpet. She’s in an enormous T-shirt from somebody’s charity 5K and flannel pajama pants printed with little cowboy boots, her face lit blue from below by the screen. She has her laptop open and held out in front of her, flat on both palms, level, the screen lit, the way you’d carry a birthday cake down a drafty hall with every candle going. Her pink BlackBerry is clamped in her teeth by one end, and buzzing. And she is, entirely by accident, right on the beat. Every open door she passes, she passes on it; her ponytail goes on it; a boy who puts his head out of 209 to see what the noise is pulls it back in on it.
She doesn’t see Jack. She gets to 217 and shoulders the door without knocking, because it’s hers, and goes in with the cake held high, and leaves the door open behind her.
It comes out of 217 and through the glass and up the well past him, Dallas at full volume: “Oh my God. *Lena.*”

And then something from Lena, lower, that might be a laugh and might be *Laney, I gave it* up; he gets the shape of it more than the words. The door of 217 swings shut on whatever comes next, and the song has the hall to itself again.

Whatever her face did, it did it on the other side of that door, and he is not going to know it today. He stands on the landing with one hand on the rail and the back of the other wrist pressed to his mouth, because his mouth has gone off and done something without consulting him, in a stairwell, on a Wednesday afternoon, with only the fire extinguisher for a witness.
He keeps going down. It hasn’t worn off by the ground floor.

s05.slug: WEDNESDAY · 5:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — THEODORE. HALL. NOW.
body: Laney arrives at speed. The door of 412 is propped on one of Theo’s loafers for the air, and she comes through the gap without slowing, BlackBerry in her fist and her hair half out of its clip, and she’s two steps toward Theo’s bed with her mouth already open on the first word when she sees Jack at his desk.

She stops. He watches her swallow it: whatever she has carried up two flights at that speed, all of it, in one gulp, like a mouthful of something too hot to hold. Her eyes water a little with the effort.
“Fireman,” she says to Jack, very sweetly.
“Laney.”
“Y’all get that rain last night?” It comes out of her in the voice of a woman reading a statement off a card with somebody standing just out of frame.
“I didn’t hear it.”
“Me neither. Slept like a baby. Like a *baby*.” She nods several times.
She can’t sit. She tries the end of Theo’s bed and is up again before the mattress has finished taking her weight. She takes a DVD off Theo’s shelf and reads the back of it with great attention.
“That’s Fassbinder,” Theo says from the bed, without lifting his head. “You’re holding it upside down.”
“I know what I’m holding.” She puts it back on the shelf upside down.
To the bed: “Theodore. Hall. Now.”

Theo gets up, steps into his loafers one at a time, including the one holding the door, and follows her out, and pulls the door to behind him. Without the shoe it doesn’t latch; it never has without a shoulder. It drifts back open a few inches, and the hall comes in through the gap.

What comes in, Jack doesn’t try to hear, and hears anyway. A squeal, high and enormous, cut off in the middle by what can only be a hand. Then Laney, in a whisper that would carry the length of a football stadium:
“*Since when?*”
“Thursday.”
“*THURSDAY?*”
And Theo, short, with nothing on it at all: “Laney. Not this week.”
Jack has heard Theo tell Laney no before, about restaurants, about a sweater, once about a cowboy hat. Not like that.

Thursday was Texas. Jack sits at his desk with his pen on *The Moviegoer* and does nothing at all with the pen. After that the hall goes quiet for a minute, the particular quiet of two people standing in it, one of whom would very much like to be screaming.
Kevin Tran goes by the gap with a laundry basket on his hip, and stops, and backs up two steps, and puts his head in. “Respectfully,” he says, “is someone being murdered?”
“Not yet,” Jack says.
Kevin nods; on this floor it’s a reasonable answer. He goes on with his basket.
Past the gap the stairwell door bangs, and a pair of socks goes down the well at a dead run.
Whatever Theo has known since Texas, Laney knows it now. And not one of them is going to say a word to him about any of it this week, because Theo said so in a hallway.

Theo comes back alone a minute later. His collar is crooked and there’s a smear of pink lip gloss high on one cheekbone, and his face is perfectly composed. He sits down on his bed, picks the screenplay up off the carpet, opens it somewhere in the middle, and looks at it.
Whatever happened out there, he has brought none of it back in with him but the lip gloss. He crosses his ankles. He licks his thumb and turns a page with it.
“Laney says hello.”

choices.text: “Is that lip gloss, or did you lose a fight with a highlighter?”
response: Theo touches his cheekbone, looks at his fingertip, and wipes it on the screenplay. “Both,” he says. “She’s very strong for her size.”
He turns a page, reads it, and turns it back.

choices.text: “Theo. Thank you.”
response: “Don’t,” Theo says, to the page. He turns it. “Okay.”
He doesn’t look up, and that’s how Jack knows it landed.

choices.text: *Let it go.*
response: They sit in it. It isn’t a bad thing to sit in. The window goes from blue to dark behind the eucalyptus, and Theo reads the same scene three or four times, and Jack doesn’t interrupt him.
Kevin goes past the door the other way, the basket full of folded laundry now, squared at the corners, and says nothing at all.

s06.slug: WEDNESDAY · 6:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — WEDNESDAY
body: He calls her. Not Sunday, and not her call; his, on a Wednesday, from his step, with the stairwell to himself and the landing glass going dark. Any other Wednesday of his life she’d pick up saying *Who died?*

He hasn’t eaten. He got as far as the Commons at four, and stood in the line with a tray, and put the tray back. He has had all day to find the words for his mother and has found the same few he had at breakfast. They’ll have to do. She has never needed many from him.

It’s half past nine on Glenwood. She picks up before the first ring is through, and the long cord rattles taut against the table leg at her end, so he knows where she has been sitting since supper. He can see the kitchen: the overhead light off and the one over the stove on, the clock above it four minutes fast since before he was born, the calendar from the funeral home by the phone with every Sunday already written on.

body.text: “You said Wednesday,” Ma says. “It’s Wednesday.”
“You said you’d write your grandmother,” Ma says. “You called instead.”
“Not on the phone, you said,” Ma says. “Well. Here’s the phone.”

body: “A little broken heart,” she says. “On the computer. Gina showed me. She walked me through it from Denver like I was landing a plane. Last time, you called me before the computer.”
“I know, Ma.”
“This time the computer called me.”
“It’s true, Ma.”

He tells her. He tells it plain, like a noise in the truck reported to his father: what, and when, and nothing on it. He ended it. Last night. There’s somebody else, and nothing happened, and he told her before anything could. Ma doesn’t stop him. The tap goes on at her end, and off.
“Nothing happened.”
“Nothing, Ma.”
“I believe you. I’m asking so I can say I asked.” A glass set down on the counter. “Did you tell her to her face?”
“Yes.”
“Good,” Ma says.

She doesn’t add anything to it. He didn’t know, till he heard it, how badly he needed somebody on this earth to say that word to him about last night. He sits on his step with it, and it’s enough to sit on.
“Are you sleeping?”
“Not last night.”
“Tonight, then. That’s not a request. How are you?”
“I’m good.”
“Don’t you *I’m good* me, Jackie. I’m your mother.” A chair leg scrapes on the linoleum; she’s sitting back down. “Was she good to you?”
“She was good to me, Ma.” It comes up out of him without his choosing it, and it’s the easiest true thing he’s said all day. “She’s the funniest person I ever met.”
“Funnier than you?”
“She’d have done your voice, Ma. In a day. The cord, the tap, all of it.”
“My voice.”
“You’d have laughed.”
“I’d have hit her with the dish towel,” Ma says. “And then I’d have laughed.” A dish goes into the rack. “Then I’m sorry. For both of you. Is somebody bringing her soup?”
“Theo went.”

“Theo,” Ma says, as though that settles the soup. “You told me she was the answer. In January, on the phone, with your grandmother praying through the wall. I never said a word back. I liked her. I never met her, and I liked her. Your grandmother had her at the table already. She had the menu.” The radiator knocks under her window. “I’m allowed to be sad about a girl I never met. It’s a free country.”
Behind her, from the chair by the radiator, Nonna says something in Calabrese. He catches *Maria Caterina* in it, and the rest he doesn’t need.
Ma takes the phone away from her mouth. “No, Mà,” she says, and a little more after it, soft, in the same Calabrese, and he doesn’t need that translated either.
Nonna says something else, short and soft. Ma does translate that.
“*Poverina,*” Ma says. “Poor little thing. She says she’ll light a candle for her Sunday. At St. Brigid’s, after the nine o’clock.”

A few weeks ago Nonna lit one for the same girl, glad, the morning she first heard the name. This one is the other kind. He can see her at it: the rack of red glass under the Blessed Mother at St. Brigid’s, Nonna feeding a folded dollar into the box with her good hand and taking a long time over the taper, not because she’s slow but because she’s telling the Blessed Mother about it, in Calabrese, in detail, a girl from California, too thin, who she never got to feed.
“She never met her, Ma.”
“She never met half the people she lights them for. That’s what they’re for.”

He puts his free hand over his eyes on the step and keeps it there. On Glenwood the radio in the front room is going low, the Italian station out of Cleveland that Nonna won’t let anybody change, and somebody is singing on it in a hurry about the sea.
“Your father’s out in the garage,” Ma says.

He can see it from here: the overhead door down against the cold, the drop light hooked under the Silverado’s hood, his father on the creeper with the drain pan, letting out oil that went in new in January so he can put new oil in after it.
“He knows?”
“I told him at supper. He didn’t say anything. He finished his plate. Then he went out there.”
“Tell him I’m good.”
“You tell him. He has a phone. He uses it like he’s mad at it.”
He hears her move the phone to her other shoulder. She does that before a thing she has been holding since supper.

body: Morro 1100 is filling the way it fills on a Thursday, from the bottom up, laptops coming open on a hundred News Feeds, coffees going down on the floor between sneakers. Dr. Fenner is at the board already with the chalk, drawing a row of little humps that march off the right-hand edge of it. Jack climbs to the back row under the exit sign.
Her seat is beside his. The fold-down desk is folded up.

On Tuesday she was somewhere over California, a window seat and a flight number, and the folded desk was the airline’s doing. She’s been back since Tuesday afternoon. She’s most likely down the bluff on Del Playa right now, in the house with the yellow boots by the door, a walk from this chair. She has missed Fenner before — for a meeting in LA, for a fitting, for a table read — and every one of those came with a city. He sets his bag on the floor at his own feet and leaves her desk the way it is.

From the back row you can see every screen in the room. A boy three tiers down is drafting a fantasy baseball team in February. Two girls in the middle are sharing one pair of earbuds, a bud each, heads tipped together. Fenner taps the chalk twice on the board and the quiet goes up the tiers from the front, row by row, till it reaches the exit sign. “Partners are partners till May,” he says, as he says every week. “No trades. I get requests.”

Somewhere down front a laptop shuts. Fenner taps the humps with the chalk. “Swell,” he says, and underlines them. “Which is what a wave turns into once it gets out from under the wind that made it.” He does fetch, the stretch of open water the wind has to work with, and duration, how long it blows, and then he turns from the board with the chalk up, pleased with the ocean. “Dispersion. Once they’re loose, the long ones outrun the short ones. By the time it gets to your beach it’s sorted itself, longest first. The sea is tidier than any of you.”

“Somewhere off the Aleutians right now,” he says, “there’s a low the size of Texas leaning on the water. You won’t feel a thing. Next week it’ll stand up off the Point at six feet on a sunny morning with no wind at all, and every surfer in this room will cut my class.” A laugh goes round the tiers, and two boys in board shorts in the fourth row look at each other with real hope.
Jack writes *fetch* in the margin and puts a box around it, and then sits with the pen on the box for most of a page of Fenner.
At twenty to twelve Fenner frees the tiers for partner conferences, sign-up sheet at the front, and the room comes apart into twos, chairs squealing round to face each other up and down the rows.
“Mr. Costigan.” Up the tiers from the lectern, cheerful, the chalk still in his hand. “Your partner?”
“Not today.”
“Tuesday, then. Put yourselves down.” He’s already turning to a girl in the front row who wants to know about Hawaii, delighted with her.

The sign-up sheet comes hand to hand along the rows and somebody passes it into the back. The term pairs are numbered down the margin in Fenner’s blocky hand. Forty-one is *Costigan / Callender*, and the line for Tuesday beside it is blank. Jack holds the clipboard for a while with the pen on its string between his fingers. Then he passes it on down the row with the line the way he found it.
The handouts are on the table by the back door, under the exit sign.

s08.slug: THURSDAY · 1:05 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — DIRECT ADDRESS
body: There’s no sun on this side of Hollis after one, and 302 gets what comes up off the water instead, a cool, even, unforgiving light that finds every ring a coffee cup ever left on the oak. The same twelve in the same chairs: Jack at the door end under the clock, Lena at the window end, Caleb beside Jack with his pens laid out in a row by color, Yusuf beside Caleb, the two sophomores from the window side, Evan at the door with the roster on its clipboard.

Hale comes in with his coffee and the soft paperback and takes his place halfway down the side, where he has to turn his head for either end. “Percy,” he says. “Still for the travellers.” He opens it to the back and doesn’t look at it. There’s a high color along his cheekbones today, and a little more Yorkshire than usual in his vowels.
“Percy will not show us one prayer of Binx Bolling’s. Not a Mass, not a sentence. Honesty or cowardice? I said on Monday I’d never decided. I’d like it decided by two-thirty.”
The table does what it does at the top of the hour, settles, waits to see who’ll go. Caleb uncaps the green.
From the window end, and not to the chair: “Youngstown.”

Every head at the table comes round. They go to the window end first and then they come up the oak to the clock, and Caleb, before he has finished turning, looks at Hale to see whether Hale has seen. Hale has. He turns a page he isn’t reading.

Lena has her sleeves pushed up to the elbow and her pencil laid across the open book like a bar across a door, and she’s looking straight up the table at him. The length of Hale’s oak is in the way, and Hale, and Caleb’s pens, and she doesn’t appear to have noticed any of it.

“You’re going to tell me he’s being honest,” she says. “So let me tell you what he did. A Catholic man writes a Catholic hero — a man who goes looking for God up and down Elysian Fields — and in two hundred and some pages he won’t let that hero speak to God where the rest of us can hear it. Not a Hail Mary at a red light. Not a Mass. Not a sentence.” She lifts the pencil off the book. “Now. When a client won’t take the stand, every lawyer at Tulane and Broad knows exactly what the jury does with that. They don’t call it humility. They go out, and they come back in twenty minutes. If you believe a thing, you say it where people can hear it, or the people who were listening carry it for you. Percy made the reader carry it. That’s cowardice, and he had the nerve to dress it up as good manners.”
Jack sits back in his chair. He has missed this more than cigarettes.
He opens Hale’s copy to the back.

Her pencil is already moving.

At the window end Lena’s pencil stops.

At the far end of the oak, Lena tips her head to him, once: the joke conceded, and not one inch of the argument.

“Three.”

“Manners. Ash Wednesday. He quotes Matthew at me.”
“They don’t talk during the picture. Lord. He’s been saving that.”
“The man conceded on the first round. Somebody check him for a fever.”

body: She turns to the end of the book without hunting for it. “The epilogue. Lonnie’s dead. And the little ones come out to the car with their questions for Binx, and the big one is this: on the last day, when everybody’s raised up, will Lonnie still be in his wheelchair?” She sets her pencil down on the page. “And Binx tells them no. Just like that. No. He answers a child. A child at a car window gets the creed, and the reader gets a shrug. That’s the evasion. He had the answer all along, and he gave it to the one person in the book who couldn’t write it down.”

He can see her hands today. It’s the first thing he notices, before he notices he’s noticing it: the pencil, which she holds like a cigarette when she’s winning, the thumb running down the edge of the page, a strand of hair going round and round one finger of the other hand without her knowing it’s there. She has been coming at him down the oak for twenty minutes and it’s better than anything on television.
“He gives it to the one who —” Jack says.
“— asked, I know, I read the same —”
“— so it isn’t a shrug. It’s got —”
“— an address on it,” she says, “and it isn’t ours,” and at the door Evan’s pen clicks once.

“And don’t you tell me that’s humility,” she says, picking it straight up again. “Humility’s saying the thing and then getting out of the way. Percy stays in the way and says nothing and calls it modesty. On my street we call it coy.”
From halfway down the side, to the ceiling, Hale says, “Don’t stop on my account.”

Jack has the page open in Hale’s copy. In the margin beside the children’s question, in the small upright pencil, Hale has written *Well*, with a period after it, which is more than he wrote beside anything else in the epilogue and less than Jack would like.

The table has stopped writing. Caleb has the green pen held up by his ear, forgotten, and he turns from one end of the oak to the other and back with his mouth a little open, as happy as Jack has ever seen a person look in a chair. Hale has put his own pencil down. He isn’t refereeing. He doesn’t appear to think he’s needed.

She looks at the clock over his head instead of at him, thinking.

Down the oak, very quietly, Yusuf: “B-minus.”

response: She sits back. It’s the face she makes when somebody tells her the truth in the middle of an argument: half pleased, half sorry about the waste of a good fight.
She writes something in her margin and doesn’t say what.

response: “With whoever’s in it,” she says back to him, slowly, weighing it.
Under the middle window the radiator knocks and gives up.

Lena lays her hand flat on the open book. “But if that’s Percy’s rule,” she says, “— a man says the true thing only to whoever happens to be in the car with him — then the rest of us had better get in the car. And that’s an imposition, and Percy knows it. He sits up front with the answer in his lap and makes the reader ride in the back the length of the book, waiting for him to turn around. Silence isn’t modest. Silence makes the reader do the work the writer wouldn’t. If I want to know what Binx believes, I have to climb in the back seat with a carload of children and wait for one of them to ask? That’s a cover charge, and Percy’s working the door.”

Jack thinks of Frank in the Silverado. Frank has never volunteered a true thing at the kitchen table. Stopped on the Market Street bridge with the wipers going, he will answer anything you ask him straight, so long as it’s just the two of you in the cab.

She waits for him. She has her chin up and the pencil going end over end under her fingers, and the table waits with her, every one of them happier watching this than doing anything else available at a quarter to two on a Thursday.
She has him in a corner, and from the look of her she knows it, and she looks sorry about it for almost no time at all.

Down the oak the sophomores are writing *imposition*. Caleb has started writing again, very fast, the green pen going and his tongue in the corner of his mouth. That’s the only thing he says about it. He gives the rest of the hour to Yusuf, who has been waiting since Monday to talk about the aunt.

At ten past two the essays come back down the oak. Jack’s comes hand to hand from Caleb — THE SECOND LINE — and he turns to the last page. Nothing in any margin. No grade. Under the last line, in the small upright hand that runs up every page of Hale’s Percy: *See me.*
It’s pencil, and small, and somehow it takes up more of the page than anything he typed. Caleb leans over to look, sees it, and sucks air in through his teeth.

Lena’s goes down the window side. She reads her last page where she sits. Something on it makes her mouth go small and pleased, and she puts her thumb over it so the sophomore beside her can’t see, and then she folds the essay in half the long way and puts it in her bag, and she doesn’t show him. He doesn’t ask.
At half past two the room comes apart, chairs going back, the sophomores in their coats before Hale has finished his sentence about Monday. Two things happen at once.

And from the head of the stairs, already going, Lena, to him: “I’m going to the Brick.”

body: Hollis 314 is at the far end of the third floor past the department copier, and its door stands open about the width of a dog. Inside it is mostly books: books in towers on the floor, books shelved two deep with the back row showing over the heads of the front, books on the one chair that isn’t Hale’s, which Hale clears by setting them on the floor as a tower of their own. Berkeley is asleep on the rug in the only square of sun, long and white at the muzzle, his ribs going up and down, and being deaf, he doesn’t stir when they come in. One ear has folded itself inside out on the rug. The sash window is propped open on a fat paperback Housman, and the room smells of dog and old paper and, faintly, last night.

Hale drops into his own chair. His reading glasses are on top of his head, where he has evidently lost them. There’s an old red half-moon of wine on his left cuff, laundered and ironed and still there.
“Sit, if you can find the chair. Give it here.”
Jack gives it to him. Hale turns to the last page and reads it to himself, not aloud, the way he reads everything at the table.

“I don’t write compliments in margins,” he says. “Students frame them. Hence *See me*.” He turns back to the first page and puts his finger on the top line. “*The band goes out slow and comes back loose.* I liked that. It writes a cheque. For four thousand words you try to cash it with cleverness, and then on the last page you simply pay.” He turns to the end again and taps the last paragraph. “The waiting. The second line goes round the block, and the people on the curb stand there, and it comes back, loose. This is the only paragraph in four thousand and twelve words in which you were not performing for me, Mr. Costigan. You were standing on a curb. Somewhere on the last page you forgot I existed, and the prose improved out of all recognition. You should be ashamed of the rest of it. It’s very clever. Clever is what a frightened man writes when he’s too vain to write a bad sentence, and at four thousand words it reads like polished shit. I could have written it, and that is not a compliment.”

body.text: That paragraph is the one he typed in one go at half past five on Sunday, on the eighth floor of the Brick, and never read back.

body: “The second line,” Hale says. “Remind me. The people who follow the band.”
“They’re not in the parade. They just come. They fall in behind the brass and go where it goes.”
“Yes, I know what it is, Mr. Costigan, I’ve been to New Orleans. I was asking whether you did.” He looks at the last page again. “Where did you write it?”

body: “Yes,” Hale says. “One can tell. The curb got into it anyway.” He turns the page to the light. “You didn’t read it over. Don’t tell me. There’s a comma missing in the third line you’d have put in if you had. Leave it out. It’s better without.”

He hands the essay back across the desk. For a moment he isn’t looking at Jack, or at the page; he’s looking past Jack’s shoulder at the window, where there’s nothing but the top of a eucalyptus and the sky behind it.
“In my experience it doesn’t always come back round the block, Mr. Costigan. Sometimes it turns off down a side street, and that’s the last you hear of the trumpets.”
And at once, to the rug: “Berkeley. Stop that.”
Berkeley, asleep in his patch of sun, goes on doing nothing whatsoever.
Hale picks a pen up off the desk and puts it down somewhere else. “Well? I haven’t got all afternoon. The dog has a constitutional.”

choices.text: “Thank you, Professor.”
response: “Don’t thank me. It’s unbecoming in a Catholic. Go away.”
On the rug, at nothing anybody can see, Berkeley’s tail thumps the floor one time.

choices.text: “So that paragraph’s an A.”
response: “That paragraph is a paragraph. The rest is brass, Mr. Costigan, and a great deal of it.”
He finds his glasses on top of his head, takes them down, and puts them on to look at Jack properly for the first time all afternoon.

choices.text: “Did it? Come back?”
response: Hale doesn’t answer. He gets up and takes the dog’s lead down off the hook on the back of the door.
“Mind the second step on your way down, Mr. Costigan. It’s loose.”

s08k.slug: THURSDAY · 3:00 PM · THE BRICK, EIGHTH FLOOR — THE CHAIR
body: Somebody on the eighth floor of the Brick is highlighting an entire textbook, and the felt tip squeaks on every line, three rows over, all afternoon. Her carrel is the one by the east window, where the water shows between two roofs. Her coat is over the back of her chair and her shoes are off under the desk, her Percy open in front of her, penciled to the margins, and a legal pad beside it, and the chair next to hers is pushed in.

body.text: He pulls it out and sits down in it. On Sunday he typed two rows back with his back to this chair, and it was empty. She reaches over without a word and moves her bag off the corner of the desk so his elbow has somewhere to go.
body.else: He pulls it out and sits down in it — his first time up on her floor since the fall — and she reaches over without a word and moves her bag off the corner of the desk so his elbow has somewhere to go.

body: “Didn’t Hale want a word?” she says, still reading.
“He said another time.”
“He’ll keep.” She turns a page. Under the desk her socks don’t match, one green, one with a brown pelican on it, and she has them hooked round the legs of her chair.

They study. That is, she studies, and he opens his Percy to the epilogue and reads the same half page about the children at the car window until he could say it back, and every so often her pencil stops and so does his reading, and he keeps his eyes on Binx.

Once her pen dies, and she reaches over blind and takes his, writes a line with it, and puts it back by his hand pointing the way it was. Out past her, the platforms stand off in the Channel with their lights not on yet, and the water between the two roofs goes from blue to a hard bright tin as the afternoon comes round. Twenty minutes of that. Then she takes the last page of her essay off the top of the pile and slides it across to him, face up, and goes straight back to her legal pad and underlines something that is already underlined.
THE NEUTRAL GROUND, the last page. In the margin, in Hale’s pencil, a single tick, and beside it, which Jack reads upside down before he turns the page the right way round: *Yes.*

It’s about the median down the middle of St. Charles, the strip with the streetcar tracks in it, where New Orleans stands to watch the parades go by. He reads to the end. The last sentence is in her voice so exactly that he can hear her say it across a table with a fork in her hand:

*On the neutral ground nobody owns the street: you stand in the middle with your mother’s folding chair and your cousin’s ladder and a cooler of Barq’s, the parade on one side of you and the rest of New Orleans on the other, and for one afternoon a city that agrees about nothing agrees about where to stand.*

When he looks up she’s found his last page, sticking out of his Percy where he shoved it, and she has it turned so she can read the bottom. *See me.* She laughs without a sound, the library laugh, and has to look out the window at the two roofs till it passes.

response: She reads it. He watches her get to the last paragraph, the second line going round the block and coming back loose, and her pencil, which goes everywhere with her, doesn’t move.
When she’s done she turns his page face down on the desk and leaves her hand on it, and goes back to her own book without taking it away.

response: “I know.” She tips her head at the page sticking out of his Percy. “Yours made him write *See me*.”
“That’s not a compliment.”
“From Hale it’s a sonnet.”

choices.text: “You wrote a whole page about standing in the middle of the street.”
choices.key: On the eighth floor of the Brick you sat in the chair beside Lena’s, read the last page of her essay, and told her she’d written a whole page about standing in the middle of the street.
response: “Best place to stand.” She takes the page back and squares it on her pad. “You see both sides go by.”
Out past her shoulder, between the two roofs, the light is coming off the water in pieces.

choices.text: *Read it twice. Hand it back. Say nothing.*
choices.key: On the eighth floor of the Brick you read the last page of Lena’s essay twice, in the chair beside hers, and handed it back without a word.
response: He goes back to the top and reads it again, slower. She watches him do it with her chin on her hand and makes no move to stop him.
When he holds it out a library cart squeaks past the end of the row, and she takes the page.

s09.slug: THURSDAY · 9:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, 4TH FLOOR LOUNGE — SOURCES SAY
body: The lounge TV is on the Olympics with the sound off, a skater in red going round a white rink under a black roof, arms out, in perfect silence. Jack came in for the vending machine. He has a bag of pretzels in his hand and he has not been permitted to leave.

Laney is perched on the arm of the couch in a quilted pink robe, with her laptop open on her knees and a pair of tortoiseshell reading glasses low on her nose that she does not need and has never needed, which is the point of them. Theo is cross-legged on the carpet in the blazer, his back against the couch. Kevin has the armchair and his organic chemistry and a highlighter, and the air of a man who was here first, and was, and would like that noted. Margot is at the far end of the couch with her notebook on her knee.

“Lena’s at the Brick,” Laney says, before anybody asks. “She’d make me stop, and she’d be right, so she’s not invited.” She pushes the glasses up her nose with one finger. “Ladies and gentlemen of the fourth floor. Our next item comes to us from the internet, where it was posted at six forty-seven this morning by a woman who has never once been right about anything in her life. She’ll be competing tonight in the category of Breaking News. Please hold your applause.”
“I’m studying,” Kevin says.
“You’re *present*, Kevin. That’s all the pageant requires.”
Not a soul was going to applaud. Theo gives her a drumroll on his thighs anyway.

body.title: A celebrity blog — Thursday, 6:47 AM
body.text:
SWEETWATER’S SKYE CALLENDER SINGLE AGAIN?! MYSTERY GUY OUT

Spotted — and spotted ALONE! *Sweetwater* sweetheart Skye Callender, 19, quietly went from “in a relationship” to nothing at all on Facebook Wednesday afternoon, and our inbox EXPLODED. A source close to the actress says the hunky mystery college boyfriend “couldn’t handle her fame,” and that the pair had been drifting ever since she began filming in Vancouver. Mystery Guy, last seen in the famous borrowed work jacket, could not be reached for comment, mostly because nobody knows his NAME. A rep for the actress did not respond to our request for comment.

body: At “Spotted — and spotted ALONE!” Theo does a camera shutter with his tongue, three frames. She reads the rest of it the way the six o’clock news reads a tornado, chin down, every word a little lower than the one before. Under SINGLE AGAIN?! Theo runs a slide whistle up through the roof of his mouth. At “the hunky mystery college boyfriend” she stops and looks at Jack over the glasses. “*Hunky*,” she says. “Honey, they have confused you with a man who’s been touched in this decade.” Back down. At “couldn’t handle her fame” Theo hits a gong — a long, shivering *bwonnng* with his hand cupped over his mouth to make it ring — and Laney stops dead and reads it again for the gong: “*Couldn’t handle her fame.*”
“Drifting,” she says, savoring it. “Since *Vancouver*.” She doesn’t look at Jack this time. He answered every one of the Vancouver calls. The blog doesn’t know that.

At “the famous borrowed work jacket” she lifts one arm and points across the lounge at the Carhartt with her wrist turned and her smile on — “and for our viewers at home, *the jacket*” — and Theo does a record scratch.
“Could not be reached for comment,” Laney says, “mostly because nobody knows his *name*. Jack, you are a mystery to the entire nation.”
Theo, on the carpet, plays a sustained low cello note on nothing, for suspense.

“It’s a genre,” Margot says, from the end of the couch, without any change in her face. “The obituary of the celebrity class. Three facts, two of them wrong, and a photograph of the deceased at an airport.”
“Funny you should say that,” says Laney. “And now, ladies and gentlemen, the evening-wear portion of the competition.” She turns the laptop around.

body.text: Tuesday at LAX — back from Vancouver and ALL SMILES. Little did we know!!

body: Skye under the arrivals sign with her bag on her shoulder and her sunglasses pushed up in her hair, mid-stride, laughing at something past the edge of the picture. From the carpet, the studio audience: *ooooh.* Jack looks at it for the length of the ooh.
“Couldn’t. Handle. Her. Fame,” says Laney, to the photo, with sorrow, and scrolls.

body.title: Photo 2 (from our archives)
body.text: Happier times: hand in hand with Mystery Guy behind a church banner in January. We’ll always have San Francisco.

body: It’s the one from the Walk in January, her hand in his behind the banner, the one the country was invited to have an opinion about. Laney gives the caption the full soap opera, a woman in a negligee at the top of a staircase: “*We’ll always have San Francisco.*” She lets it hang there, and scrolls on to the comments.

body.text:
Did he dump her?? Did SHE dump HIM?? Is Cassidy single too?? Sound off below!

body: She does them in voices. The first is a girl from somewhere with a lot of malls, in capitals, furious: “SKYE CALLENDER IS TOO GOOD FOR EVERY MAN ON EARTH. EVERY SINGLE ONE. I CHECKED.” The second is a Valley drawl, very bored: “ok so i go to marisol and i have SEEN mystery guy and he is not a hunk. he is a guy with a dishrag. like an actual dishrag. on his shoulder.”
“That one’s accurate,” Margot says.
Laney looks at Jack across the lounge for a long, appraising moment. She scrolls all the way back up to the top, to read it one more time, with feeling: “*Couldn’t handle her fame.*”
“Respectfully, Laney,” Kevin says, turning a page of his chemistry, “that’s the fourth time you’ve read ‘couldn’t handle her fame.’”

“It’s the best line in it, Kevin.” She scrolls back down. The third one she reads in her own voice, no voice at all, quick and even: “praying for you skye. the Lord is close to the brokenhearted. psalm 34.” She goes past it without stopping. “Two hundred and nine more,” she announces, “and I have *all night*.”
Jack opens the pretzels. It seems the thing to do.

response: “Sugar, nobody in Ohio has *met* you.” She doesn’t look up from the screen to say it.

choices.text: “She’d laugh at this harder than you, Laney. Not this week, though.”

response: “I know she would,” Laney says, to the laptop, and scrolls on before anybody can look at her.

choices.text: “Every word of that’s wrong. Keep going.”
choices.key: When Laney read the gossip blog aloud, you told the room every word of it was wrong — and told her to keep going.
response: “Oh, I *intend* to.”
She shakes out her hair and slides the prop glasses back down her nose, back from the commercial break.

choices.text: *Sit on the arm of the couch and let her finish.*
choices.key: When Laney read the gossip blog aloud, you sat on the arm of the couch and let her finish.
response: He sits on the other arm of the couch, and Laney turns on the cushion to face him and does the next six comments to him and him alone, a command performance, a different woman for every one: a Long Island aunt, a cheerleader, a lady from church who has *heard things*.
At the end she waits, chin up, eyes on the middle distance, for the judges.

s09a.slug: THURSDAY · 9:55 PM · DELGADO HALL, 4TH FLOOR LOUNGE — PHOTO 3
body: Laney scrolls past the end of the comments, to where the blog has stuck one more picture at the very bottom.
