body: It’s small, and taken from across the street past the side mirror of a parked car, and a little crooked. Skye on the Las Olas sidewalk under the jasmine, in sunglasses, a paper cup in one hand, her hair down and blowing. A man’s flannel shirt on her with the cuffs turned back twice, coming down to the middle of her thighs, the plaid gone soft at the elbows. Two buttons gone.
He knows it. He knew it before the picture had finished loading, line by line, down the screen. That shirt has been through the wash on Glenwood Avenue more times than he has.
There’s no sound effect. There hasn’t been one from the carpet since the second photo.
Laney glances up from the screen and catches him knowing it. She goes back to the photo and stays on it one second longer than the bit needs.
Then she closes the laptop.
“That’s enough of that.”

She takes the glasses off and folds them and puts them in the pocket of her robe, and sets the shut laptop on the cushion beside her and pats it twice, the way you’d settle a dog. Kevin caps his highlighter. Margot’s notebook stays shut on her knee.

On the TV the skater in red comes out of her last spin and stops dead in the middle of the white ice with both arms up over her head, and the arena stands up for her without a sound, and Kevin reaches over the arm of his chair for the remote and turns it off.

s10.slug: FRIDAY · 12:15 PM · ANACAPA COMMONS — THE WINDOW TABLE
body: Noon comes into the Commons off the water, white and hard, through the long windows behind the window table, and lies across the trays as far as the soft-serve machine. The fog burned off by ten. Out past the bluff the Channel is a flat bright blue with a tanker parked on it, and the radio over the dish return is playing something with a drum machine in it, low, under the noise of the trays.

body.text: On Lena’s tray there is the heel of a baguette and a glass of tap water with a handful of the machine’s ice going cloudy in it. On his there is the other heel of the same baguette, which he watched her pick out of the basket before he took the next one, and the same glass of water, and the same ice, because the machine gave it to him before he could stop it.
body.else: On Lena’s tray there is the heel of a baguette and a glass of tap water with a handful of the machine’s ice going cloudy in it. On his there is the Friday cheese pizza, a square of it gone orange at the corners, which he hasn’t touched yet, out of something like manners, and a glass of water with the same ice.

body.text: Last Friday he toasted her with a roll from the far side of the room.
Last Friday he held a plastic tumbler up at her from the far side of the room until she put hers down first.
Last Friday he ate his roll on the far side of the room and didn’t look up.

body: Today she was at the window table first, with the Pacific behind her head, and when she saw him in line with his tray she put her boot against the leg of the other chair and pushed it out from the table. That was the whole invitation. He sat in it.
There’s a basket of butter pats on the condiment cart by the window. He has looked at it twice.
“Don’t,” Lena says, without looking up from her bread.
“I wasn’t.”
“You looked at the butter. Twice.”
“Butter’s a condiment. Condiments don’t count.”

She puts her bread down on the tray to have both hands free, and he knows he’s in for it. “Butter is not a condiment. Ketchup is a condiment. Mustard is a condiment. Butter is a *foundation*. You don’t put butter *on* a thing, you build on it. There are women in St. Martin Parish who would cross the Atchafalaya on foot to slap you for that sentence, and I would hold their pocketbooks.”
“It’s dairy. It’s basically a beverage.”
“Lord have mercy.” She picks the bread back up. “Eat your water.”

He eats his water. That is, he puts a piece of the machine’s ice in his mouth and crunches it, because his hands have nothing to do on a Friday and his mouth has less, and the crunch goes off in his head like a shot in a quiet house. She stops chewing and looks at him.
“It’s water,” he says.
“Ice is water with ambitions, Youngstown.”
It comes across the tray without any warning, in the voice she used for it before there were rules, and he has to keep his eyes on his glass. “So it’s allowed.”
“It’s allowed. It isn’t humble.”

Behind her, by the doors, the waffle station is doing the noon rush: a line six deep, the iron hissing open and shut, the smell of hot batter and vanilla coming across the room in waves you could lean on. They both look at it. It is a Friday in Lent and they have been up since six and the smell is a kind of weather.
“The Desert Fathers,” Lena says, “lived on bread and salt, and a little oil on feast days, and some of them lived to a hundred. Not one of them had to sit downwind of a Belgian waffle iron.”
“Anthony had demons.”
“Anthony had demons. We have a waffle station with a *line*.” Her stomach makes a sound, short and indignant, under the table. She doesn’t blink. “That wasn’t me.”
“That wasn’t me either.”
“Then we agree it was Theo.”

Theo is at the next table, near enough to pass salt, with Laney and Kevin and Margot, all four of them having lunch with enormous discretion. Laney is looking at the ceiling. Kevin is looking at his soup. Theo is eating a tuna sandwich and appears to find it absorbing. Margot has turned her chair to face them and is simply watching, chin up, with her spoon in the air.
“Y’all are on a date at a soup kitchen,” Laney tells the ceiling.
“It’s not a date,” Lena says.

“I *know* it’s not a date.” Laney brings her eyes down from the ceiling one tile at a time. “I’d have been *told*.” She turns in her chair, all the way to them now, the bit coming over her like a spotlight. “And who’d have told me, Lena? *Facebook?* Some people have given up the entire internet for Lent and can’t even *see* it. Do you know what my week has been? I’m Paul Revere. I’m running up and down halls. I’m the only woman on the second floor who knows anything, and I have to deliver it *by hand*.”
“I hear about it,” Lena says.
“From *me*.”
“That’s what I said.”

Kevin watches Jack put another piece of ice in his mouth. “Pagophagia,” he says. “Compulsive ice-chewing. Usually it means you’re low on iron.” He looks over at the window table. “That’s not a fast, that’s a hunger strike with a seating chart.”
Theo finishes the first half of his sandwich, and starts on the second half, and says nothing about anybody.

Lena tears a corner off her heel and eats it, slowly, the way you eat a thing when it’s all there is and you mean to have all of it. She drinks some water. The light off the Channel is on the side of her face, and on the medal, and on the crumbs on her tray, and she hasn’t once looked like a woman suffering anything at him. He hasn’t either. He has sat across a lot of tables from her since August. This is the first one with nobody else’s name sitting at it with them, and he is so hungry he could eat the tray, and he would not be anywhere else in California.

choices.text: *Raise your heel of bread to her. Across eighteen inches this time.*
response: He lifts the heel off his tray and raises it to her, a beer at a ballgame, the crust end up.
She looks at it. She looks at him. She lifts hers, gravely, between her finger and thumb, and holds it up to his, and the two pieces of bread stop short of each other over the trays and don’t touch.
At the next table Laney puts her face in her hands.

choices.text: “Seven.”
response: She doesn’t look up. “I know what time the Stations are.” She brushes a crumb off the tray with the side of her hand, and lets him sit in it a moment. “I’m the one who told you.”
She takes a bite of bread and chews it, looking out at the tanker on the Channel with great composure.

choices.text: *Tear yours in half and trade her the better end.*
response: He tears his heel in half down the middle, which a baguette heel does not want to do, and it fights him and sheds, and he holds out the half with more of the soft inside in it and less of the end.
She takes it and turns it over and examines it, crust and crumb and tear, like a nun reading a permission slip. She keeps it. She hands him hers, which is worse.
At the next table Margot uncaps her pen over the open notebook, and holds it there, and writes nothing down, conspicuously.

s11.slug: FRIDAY · 7:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — STATIONS OF THE CROSS
body: Overhead the church is a boat turned keel-up on the hill, the Douglas-fir ribs going up out of the side walls in two long rows and meeting in the dark at the top, and on a Friday night in Lent forty people walk around inside the hull of it. The windows have only Ocean Road behind them at this hour. The blue glass is nearly black, keeping a little of its color only where the side lamps reach it, a deep cold blue like the bottom of a swimming pool at night.

There’s purple on the ambo and purple on the cloth at Mary’s feet and purple on the stole around Father Osei’s neck as he comes out of the sacristy behind the processional cross. A tall quiet sophomore from the nine o’clock carries it, and two acolytes come after him with candles. At the first station the cross stops, and Father Osei names it to the carving on the wall, *Jesus is condemned to death*, and reads the little meditation about the basin and the washed hands like news about a man he knew, and says, “We adore you, O Christ, and we praise you,” and forty people go down on one knee on the tile and answer, “Because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world,” Mrs. Fitch a half-step out in front of the rest of them, as she is every Friday.
Lena is up front in the black lace, at the head of the little crowd, where the cross is.
Jack is at the back of the crowd, not the back of the church. When the cross turns from the first station toward the second, he goes with it.

He walked these at St. Brigid’s on Friday nights with Nonna’s hand on the back of his neck, before he was tall enough to see the carvings over the heads in front of him, and they haven’t gotten any easier to look at since. He has stopped expecting them to.

body.text: He hasn’t eaten since noon, half a heel of bread, and the hunger has gone up out of his stomach into his head, a high clean ringing that puts sharp edges on the candle flames.
body.else: He ate at noon, and it hasn’t done much; the day has gone up out of his stomach into his head anyway, a high ringing that puts sharp edges on the candle flames.

body: At the first station, going down to the tile, his right hand goes to the breast pocket of the Carhartt, to the flat shape of the pack under the canvas, and stops there with two fingers on the button. He takes it back. He puts it on his knee, and gets up with the rest of them.

At the second station, *Jesus takes up his cross*, he’s beside an old man in a brown suit gone big on him at the shoulders, who gets down to one knee with a hand on the end of a pew and then can’t find a pew to get back up by. Jack gives him an arm. The old man takes it without looking at him, with the grip of somebody who lifted things for a living once, and comes up, and lets go. At the third he needs it again, and Jack is there, and after that it’s where Jack’s arm goes whenever the church kneels.

Between the stations, while the cross turns from one carving to the next with a noise of shoes and kneelers, Gus Ferreira gives a chord from the loft with the soft stops out and the church sings a verse of the old hymn: *At the cross her station keeping, / stood the mournful Mother weeping, / close to Jesus to the last.* Gus takes it lower than anybody, out of a chest that has spent a working life yelling across wet decks in weather, and the rest of them lean on him.

At the turns, the length of the nave ahead of him, he can see the lace. The back of her coat. At the corner by the sanctuary, her face in profile for the space of a verse, eyes down on the booklet, her lips a hair behind the response like everybody else’s. The cross goes on along the north wall, and she goes with it, and he looks at the carving in front of him, because that is what he came for.

Father Osei reads the meditations out of the booklet in the voice he uses for the parish announcements, unhurried, and doesn’t hurry the kneeling, and his left leg makes him slow at the corners, and he lets it. His eyes go to the carvings and the booklet and the floor in front of the cross, and not to anyone in the pews.

The stations go round the walls, dark carved wood, seven to a side, and he walks them. Somewhere along the walls one of them stops him, and the rest of the church goes on kneeling and rising around him while he stays in it.

choices.text: *The fourth: Jesus meets his mother.*
response: In the carving she has both her hands out toward him and can’t reach, because there is a soldier’s arm in the way, and the beam on his shoulder, and the crowd. Father Osei reads that she couldn’t take any of it from him, so she walked beside it.

Jack thinks of Ma on Wednesday night, the long cord across the kitchen, and *Good*, when he told her. He says a Hail Mary for her, a whole one, at the kitchen table in his head, and gets to *now*, and stops there with her.
The cross turns toward the fifth, and the verse begins again.

choices.text: *The eighth: the women of Jerusalem.*
response: In the carving the women have their hands up over their faces, and he has turned his head to them under the beam, on the way to it, to tell them something. Father Osei reads it short, the station’s own words out of Luke: *Do not weep for me.* Weep for yourselves, and for your children.
Jack prays for a house on Del Playa. He doesn’t know what to ask for it and doesn’t pretend to. He puts the house there, the steps and the light over the door, and leaves it in front of Him.
When the church gets up, he gets up with it. Ahead of him the acolytes walk their candles on toward the ninth, the two flames leaning back from the going.

choices.text: *The twelfth, and nothing to think at all.*
response: *Jesus dies on the cross.* At the twelfth the church kneels on the bare floor and doesn’t get up; that’s the custom here, and Father Osei doesn’t read anything for a while.

Jack kneels on the tile with his hands open on his thighs. He came in with things to say, a whole week’s worth, and at the twelfth he can’t find one of them. He has nothing to bring to it. He brings that. The quiet goes on long enough to hear the building tick as it cools, and somebody’s stomach, and nobody laughs.
From the loft Gus’s organ comes back in under the silence, a single low note held a long time, and after it, the verse.

s12.slug: FRIDAY · 7:50 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE FRONT STEPS
body: After the fourteenth and the closing prayer the forty find their coats, and the doors go open on the cold.

Outside it’s clear, the kind of cold California keeps for after dark in February, and the moon is up over the Grove across the road, a night short of full, laying the eucalyptus out in silver and black. The little crowd goes down the steps in twos and threes: two nurses from the hospital with their scrubs showing under their parkas, the man in the Cal Poly jacket who comes every Friday by himself and leaves by himself. At the curb on Ocean Road a minivan sits idling with its windows down and WHO DAT still ghosting through the road dust on its back glass.

Lena comes out ahead of him and stops on the top step, in the long yellow shape the doorway lays down the concrete, to button her coat. She does the long dark coat from the bottom up and leaves the top two, so the medal is there at her collarbone on its chain, catching some of the light from the doors. She reaches up and takes the lace off her hair, one pin and another, and folds it in half, and in half again, small enough to go in a fist.
Jack stops two steps below her. It puts her eyes level with his.

The last of the forty go down past them on either side. Mrs. Fitch, at the rail, working her driving gloves back on a finger at a time, looks from one of them to the other and back. “Goodnight, you two,” she says, and goes on down, a step at a time, holding on.

His hands are in the side pockets of the Carhartt. He takes them out, because it seems to him a man ought to have his hands out for this, and then they hang there at his sides with nothing in them. Up close in the door light her cheeks are pink with the cold. There’s a bobby pin still in her hair above one ear, forgotten, catching the light, and the folded lace is in her right fist, and she hasn’t put either hand in a pocket.

Down the hill past the Grove the Channel is a long sheet of moon with the platform lights sitting out on it. Somewhere in the church behind her Gus is closing up the organ, and the lid comes down on the keys with a wooden knock that carries out the doors. A car goes by below with its radio up and takes its song away with it. Jack is very hungry and very awake, and he can feel his heart in the ends of his fingers. She has never looked like this to him; or she has always looked like this, and he was never allowed to stand this near and look, and he isn’t sure there’s a difference.

The steps are poured concrete, the edges worn round by Catholics late for Mass since Kennedy, with a crack across one of them that somebody filled with tar and somebody else’s heels have been picking at ever since. Behind her, through the open doors, Father Osei is putting out the nave lights from the switch plate by the sacristy, bank by bank, and each time a bank goes, the blue glass in the front of the church gives up a little more of its blue.

He had it worked out at the sink in the fourth-floor bathroom on Wednesday, and on the walk to Morro, and lying on his back at two this morning looking at the ceiling of 412, and every time it came out longer, with more in front of it to get him started. One version began in August. One had Chesterton in it. One, around three, had something close to a diagram. Her eyes go past his shoulder to the street, once, and come back to him perfectly serious. She is looking at him over the folded lace, waiting. Her face says she has a fair idea what’s coming and has no intention of helping.
He leaves everything he had in front of it on the step.

choices.text: “I want to be with you. Not anybody’s anything. With you. Will you?”
choices.cue: Lena will remember how you asked.
choices.key: On the steps of St. Brendan’s after the Stations, you asked Lena to be with you — not anybody’s anything; with you.
response: He says it to her eyes, with his hands at his sides: no joke at the front of it to get him going and none at the back to get him out. At *Will you* his voice goes up at the end, the way a real question does, and he lets it.
“No.”

choices.text: “I’ve been advised to do this properly. Magdalena Thérèse Broussard, would you consider going with a dishwasher from Ohio?”
choices.cue: Lena will remember how you asked.
choices.key: On the steps of St. Brendan’s after the Stations, you asked Lena, by her whole name, whether she’d consider going with a dishwasher from Ohio.
response: He gives her every syllable of the name, *Thérèse* and all, with a small bow from the neck, and *going with* the way the old people on Glenwood Avenue still say it about a couple at the Lenten fish fry. It’s a bit when it starts. Somewhere around *dishwasher* it stops being one, and his voice gets there before he does.
“No.”

choices.text: “Be with me.”
choices.cue: Lena will remember how you asked.
choices.key: On the steps of St. Brendan’s after the Stations, you asked Lena plainly: Be with me.
response: Nothing around it. He doesn’t take a step to say it, or lift a hand. He stands where he is on the cold concrete and says it to her, low, and doesn’t add a thing.
“No.”

body: It gets to him in the half second before he can see her face, and the half second is enough.

Everything he has carried up the hill since Wednesday stops dead in his chest, a line at Lordstown when somebody hits the red button: every car on it stopped where it hangs, and the whole plant gone quiet. His throat shuts on the next thing he had to say, and there isn’t a next thing; there wasn’t supposed to be one. He has had that word from her since August in every voice she owns, across tables, up stairwells, in pencil in a margin, and in the half second all of them come back at once and stand on the step with this one.

Behind him, down on Ocean Road, a sliding door rolls shut. An engine comes up off idle. He hears it before he understands it, and looks round, and it’s Kevin’s mother’s Odyssey pulling away from the curb, not fast and not slow, at precisely the speed limit, with its blinker on, and in the side window under the streetlight, for one frame, Laney, both hands clapped over her mouth. WHO DAT goes by on the back glass, and the van goes off down Ocean Road toward campus with its taillights getting smaller.
He looks back up at Lena.

Her face is perfectly level. Chin up, mouth composed, brows not doing a thing, eyes steady on his: the face she keeps for Hale when Hale is wrong and hasn’t found out yet. It holds one more second. For Lena Broussard that is a very long time.
And then it doesn’t.

It goes at the corners first. Her mouth goes and her eyes go with it, and then she’s laughing, at him, at whatever his face has been doing since the word, the laugh with every sound in it, from low down, and it goes out over the steps and out over Ocean Road after the van.
“Was that Kevin’s *mama’s* van?”
“Doing exactly twenty-five,” Jack hears himself say, and that finishes her.

He starts to laugh too, he can’t help it, on the steps of a church after the Stations of the Cross with the moon up and his heart still trying to find where it left off. She watches him get there. She’s still laughing when she says the rest, but the laugh goes up above it somewhere and leaves it standing plain and level underneath, every word set down where she means it to go.
“Ask me to dinner, Costigan. Then ask me again. Then ask me.”
“Okay,” he says. It comes out with a laugh cracked down the middle of it that he didn’t put there. “Yeah. Okay. I can do that.”
And then there aren’t any steps between them. He’s going up to her and she’s already coming down to him.

Her face is cold. That’s the first thing: her cheek under his palm, cold from standing out on the top step, and then his hand finds her jaw and goes on past it, into the hair at the back of her neck, where it’s warm, where the lace was all through the Stations. Her mouth is cold too, at the start. Then it isn’t. She’s still smiling when it begins; he can feel the smile against his mouth, and then he can’t, because she has stopped smiling to kiss him back, and that takes all of her. The folded lace is in her fist, and the fist is up against his collar with the knuckles hard against his neck. Her other hand comes up flat on the front of the Carhartt, over the breast pocket and what’s in it, and stays there. His own free hand has found the small of her back, over the wool of the coat, and keeps to it.

He wants her. He has wanted her since a morning at the end of August, and he has spent every month since finding out how many ways there are not to, and none of them is happening now. It isn’t careful and it isn’t for anybody; there’s nobody left on the steps, and he wouldn’t know if there were. Where his wrist crosses her collarbone the medal is pressed between his skin and hers, a small hard coin of cold, and it goes warm while he isn’t paying attention. Somewhere behind her another bank of lights goes out, and he knows it only because the dark behind his eyelids gets darker.
It goes on long enough for him to stop thinking in sentences. It doesn’t go on long enough for him to forget whose steps these are.

She’s the one who breaks it. She doesn’t go far. She pulls back just enough to take her mouth off his and leaves her forehead against his forehead, and keeps it there. Their breath goes up white in the light from the doors, his and hers, and there’s no telling whose is whose.

He keeps his eyes open. He’s near enough to see that the cold has made her lashes wet at the corners, and that a strand of her hair has got caught between his forehead and hers, and he leaves it. Her coat smells of the church, candle wax and cold wood, and under that of her.
Her eyes are open, very close, and laughing at him.
“You’re being very familiar, Costigan,” she murmurs, “for a man who hasn’t asked me on a date yet.”

choices.text: “Then let me ask you.”
choices.key: With your forehead against Lena’s after your first kiss, you asked to ask her — and she told you properly means not the same night.
response: “Not tonight, Costigan. *Lord.* Properly means not the same night.”
She’s laughing again, very low, so that he feels it in her forehead more than he hears it, and she doesn’t take her forehead off his.

choices.text: “I’ve been told there are forms.”
choices.key: With your forehead against Lena’s after your first kiss, you told her you’d heard there were forms. There are so many forms, she said.
response: “There are *so* many forms.” She says it like a woman who drafted every one of them herself, in triplicate, and has the carbons in her pocketbook.
Behind her the last bank of lights goes out and the blue glass goes black, and what’s left is the streetlight from Ocean Road, and her eyes in it.

choices.text: “I’ve been familiar with you since August. I just never said.”
choices.key: With your forehead against Lena’s after your first kiss, you told her you’d been familiar with her since August and had just never said.
response: She has nothing to say back to that. He feels her start to; her forehead moves against his, and her mouth opens, and nothing comes, and she shuts it again.
Her hand on the front of the Carhartt closes on a fistful of canvas.

choices.text: *Stay where you are, foreheads touching, and say nothing.*
choices.key: With your forehead against Lena’s after your first kiss, you stayed where you were and said nothing, and she called it a good answer.
response: So he says nothing. The cold comes up off the concrete through his boots. Somewhere out on the Mesa a car downshifts for the hill. She lets the quiet run until it’s nearly a question, and then she lets it run past that.
“Good answer,” she says.

body: The church is dark behind them when they go down the steps. Father Osei hasn’t come out. They go down side by side, not touching, Lena with the lace in her coat pocket now and her hands in after it, and at the bottom they stand at the corner of Ocean Road and wait for the light, which takes its time.

The street is empty in both directions. Kevin’s mother’s van is long gone. Across the road the Grove stands up black, and the moon is over it, white enough to make the streetlights look like they’re only trying, and the eucalyptus send their smell down across the asphalt, menthol and cold and something under it like a cat that has been somewhere it shouldn’t.
The light changes. Stepping off the curb, her hand finds his.

Her fingers are cold. His aren’t steady. She doesn’t seem to mind about that, and keeps his hand anyway, and takes a better grip on it in the middle of the crosswalk, as if she has decided something about the fit, and they go over Ocean Road like that, inside the white lines, not fast.
“Your hand’s shaking,” she says, halfway over.
“It’s Lent.”
“That is not Lent, Costigan. That is something else.”
“It’s a little bit Lent.”

On the far curb she puts their two hands into the side pocket of his Carhartt, out of the cold, without a word about it, as though that’s where the two of them have always been kept. There’s a gumband in there, and a receipt from the Anchor, and her fingers find both and leave them be.

They take the path past the bike racks and along the dark edge of the Commons lawn, under the trees, and he doesn’t let go of her for anything, not to fix his collar, not to point at the moon, and she doesn’t either. A kid on a bike comes down the path toward them with a headlamp strapped to his helmet, swings wide around the two of them on the grass, and rings his bell at them, one bright ding, and is gone up the path. Off toward Las Olas somebody’s Friday is getting going, a bass line through a wall. He couldn’t tell you afterward what else they said. Her thumb moves once across his knuckles, and he would be able to tell you about that in detail for the rest of his life.
The trees open and there’s Delgado, a grid of windows, most of them lit on a Friday night, and on four, near the east end, one window lit low and flickering, with the blinds all the way up.
They both look up at it. What’s behind it, they don’t say.

body.text: On the levee he told her they’d thrown the towel in, in Arizona, and picked it back up. *With a coconut,* she said.
On the levee he said somebody ought to send them a fruit basket, and she said a *bill*.
On the levee they laughed about the pair of them till it hurt.

body: “He signaled,” Lena says, to the window, still not over it.
“He always signals.”
“At a *getaway*.”

In the east stairwell the tube light is humming over the landing, and the wired glass is black. On two, where her door is, she doesn’t let go. On three she doesn’t. On the fourth-floor landing she lets go of his hand to push the door, and down the hall, from somewhere near the end of it, something orchestral and enormous is playing, strings, a great many of them, slow, at a volume nobody plays anything at on a Friday in Lent.

s13.slug: FRIDAY · 8:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — THE WAKE
body: Halfway down the hall the music is mostly strings, and by 412 it’s nothing but strings, one long slow climb that never quite gets to the top of itself. The door is propped wide with Theo’s box set of Kurosawa. Somebody has killed the overhead. The room is lit by Jack’s desk lamp turned to face the wall and by a dozen battery tea lights along the windowsill, flickering on their little circuits, because the fire code is the fire code, even in grief.
Theo’s MacBook is open on his desk at a volume Residential Life would take an interest in.

On Jack’s desk, on a paper tablecloth, there is a funeral spread from the Texas school of grief, laid out for a party and put into black on short notice. Two dozen deviled eggs in the hollows of a milk-glass egg plate that came from Dallas, by the look of it, for exactly this. A seven-layer dip in a Pyrex dish, the layers showing through the side like a road cut on the turnpike. A pound cake on a paper doily with one slice gone. No ham. No little smoked sausages in a crockpot.
“It’s *Friday*, Kevin,” Laney is saying. “I’m not a *heathen*.”

She’s on the end of Theo’s bed in a black dress with a black cardigan over it and the sunglasses from Sunday, big and black, back for an occasion. Her ankles are crossed. She holds a cocktail napkin balled in one hand at the ready, a widow’s handkerchief at a graveside, for whenever it comes.

Kevin has wheeled his own desk chair down from 420 and sits forward on it in his jacket, zipped, with his mother’s keys in his hand: the Odyssey’s fat Honda key and a little brass Our Lady of La Vang on the ring, turning. Margot is on the floor with her back against Jack’s bed frame and her notebook open on her knee and her pen capped; so far the page has the date on it and nothing else. And on Theo’s desk beside the laptop, unopened, laid out on a folded white Delgado towel with the yellow label turned to the room, is a bottle of Veuve Clicquot, the guest of honor at an open casket.
Theo is on his feet in the middle of the room in the blazer, one hand on the back of his desk chair like a lectern, delivering.

“Picture it —” Theo says. “A man. A staircase. A long time. Longer than the studio wanted; the studio sent notes. He climbs it. He sits on it. He gives up smoking on it, for God, in front of everybody. Every night he’s on those stairs and every night she’s two floors down, and the audience is throwing Junior Mints at the screen.” He breaks off. “It’s from *Platoon*,” he explains, of the strings, to nobody, and picks it back up without losing his place. “Third act. Friday night. Church steps. A moon you could read by. He asks her. And she looks at him, and she says the shortest line in the English language. You can’t cut around it. Smash to black. No sequel. Sundance passes.” He bows his head. “He was a good man. He wore the same jacket every day of his life.”
Laney touches the napkin under her sunglasses to an eye that is perfectly dry.

Margot sees them first. Then Kevin, whose keys stop turning. Then Laney, and last Theo, who comes round with his hand still on the chair. Jack in the doorway, in the jacket. Lena at his shoulder, half a step behind, her coat buttoned to the collar and her face composed for church.
Not a soul in the room says anything. On Theo’s desk the Adagio reaches the place where it swells, and swells, and goes on swelling, as if it has heard about all of this and would like to help.
He can feel Lena behind him not laughing. It comes off her like heat through a furnace wall. He lets the strings get most of the way up.
“She turned me down,” he says.
Theo and Laney turn on Lena at the same instant, with the same face.
“What the fuck, Lena?”

choices.text: *Let it run another round.*
response: He leans on the doorframe and lets them have her.

Laney gets to her feet for it, sunglasses and all. “Magdalena Broussard. On the steps of a house of God. On a *Friday*. In *Lent*. In front of witnesses and a Honda Odyssey. I did not ride across this town at twenty-five miles an hour in a minivan to stand here and call that *manners*.” Theo takes it up before she has sat back down. “Eleven hundred films, Broussard. Not one of them — not the French ones, not the ones where everybody dies on a staircase — has the girl say no on church steps under a moon like that. It’s structurally indefensible.” He lays a hand flat on the blazer. “I speak for cinema.”
Lena takes all of it with her chin up and her bare hands folded in front of her coat, like a saint in a niche who has heard worse.
When Theo is done he reaches over to the laptop without looking and turns the Adagio up.

choices.text: “Hey. Easy. She’s allowed.”
response: “Hey,” he says. “Easy. She’s allowed.”
“She is *not* allowed,” Laney says. “I deviled *eggs*.”
“There is a *bottle*, Costigan,” Theo says, from his lectern, with feeling, and turns his hand toward the desk in a slow pan: the eggs, the dip, the cake, the Veuve in state.
Beside him Lena turns her head and looks at Jack sideways, from very close, as if she’d forgotten he would do that.

choices.text: “She did turn me down. Technically.”
response: “She did turn me down,” he says. “Technically.”
Laney’s sunglasses come down her nose. Over the top of them, pure Highland Park: “*Technically?*”
Kevin, who has held very still in his chair since the doorway, closes his eyes.
“Define technically,” Theo says. “Slowly. For the bereaved.”

s13a.slug: FRIDAY · 8:35 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — EXTRA FORMS
body: Lena holds out longer than he would have bet. Her mouth stays where she put it through the strings and the eggs and the sunglasses, through all of it, and then one corner gets away from her, and she turns her face into the doorframe and her shoulders start to go.

That finishes Jack. He laughs until he has to sit down on the end of his own bed beside Kevin’s knees, and Kevin moves the keys to his other hand to make room. In the doorway Lena has one hand flat over her eyes and is making a sound like a kettle somebody forgot on the back of the stove. It goes on for some time. Every time it might be over, one of them looks at the champagne.
“Somebody,” Laney says, “had better start talking, fireman. In English. Right now.”
Lena comes in off the doorframe, wiping under one eye with the side of a finger, and undoes the top button of her coat.
“He asked me,” she says. “On the steps. And I said no.”
Laney opens her mouth. Lena puts a hand up, and it stays shut.

“Because he waited too long the first time.” She says it to the room, and it’s Jack she’s looking at, and there’s nothing in it that cuts; she might be telling them the price of shrimp. “So he gets one no, cher. It’s good for a man, once.” She smooths the front of her coat. “And then I told him how a thing like that is done, and I have agreed to let him take me to dinner. And we’ll see how it goes.”
Theo and Laney look at each other across the deviled eggs. It’s a long look, and a good deal goes back and forth in it.
“That’s a yes with extra forms,” Theo says.
“We’ll see how it goes,” says Lena, smiling so wide it has nowhere left to go.
Laney rises. She collects the Veuve off its towel in both arms and carries it across the room past Lena toward the mini-fridge under Theo’s desk, and Lena’s eyes go with it, and narrow.
“You *bought* that?” she says. “When?”

Laney crouches, opens the little fridge on Theo’s San Pellegrino and a Cool Whip tub of something from before Christmas that nobody in 412 has the courage to open, and lays the bottle in on its side between the two like a baby in a bassinet. “This,” she announces, “stays in here until there’s a yes without an asterisk.” She shuts the door with her hip and turns to the spread, too fast. “Has everybody had an egg? Kevin, you haven’t had an egg. Margot. Egg.”

body.text: The guests of honor don’t get an egg. They’ve had a heel of bread apiece since morning and tap water, and it’s Friday till midnight, and they sit side by side on the end of Jack’s bed with Laney’s deviled eggs at their knees and can’t touch a thing.
body.else: Lena has had a heel of bread and tap water since morning, and it’s Friday till midnight. Jack had the cheese pizza at noon, and he is not going to eat a deviled egg beside a woman on bread and water. They sit side by side on the end of his bed with Laney’s deviled eggs at their knees and don’t touch them.

body: Her coat sleeve lies against his from the shoulder to the elbow, and stays there, and in this room, of all rooms, not one person mentions it.
The champagne couldn’t be opened tonight if they begged: there’s the asterisk, and there’s the fast, and either one would do.

And the Adagio, which has been on repeat since a little before eight, comes back round to the beginning and starts its long climb again, and gets most of the way up, and Theo crosses the room mid-swell and stops it with one finger, with dignity. The quiet it leaves is enormous. The hall comes in through the propped door: somebody’s shower running, somebody laughing three rooms down at something else entirely.

“I was told this was a vigil,” Kevin says, to his keys. “I said leave it alone. I said it at the light on Ocean Road.” He leans over, takes a deviled egg off the milk glass, and eats it in one bite, on principle, looking at no one.
Margot uncaps her pen. “Field note,” she says, writing it as she says it. “The deceased attended her own wake. Declined refreshments. Interment postponed pending paperwork.” She caps the pen.

After that it’s just an evening. Laney’s dip goes down through the guacamole to the beans. “It was a *celebration* dip,” she tells Margot, who hasn’t asked. “It got reassigned.” Theo tells the getaway from the van’s side as an action picture, on his feet, with the desk chair for the Odyssey: Kevin at ten and two with his knuckles white, Margot taking notes in the way-back, Laney at the side window with both hands over her mouth, and the blinker going the whole length of Ocean Road, *tick, tick, tick*, “like a man defusing a bomb by the manual.” At the blinker Lena puts her face against Jack’s shoulder, and leaves it there a second longer than the joke needs. A little after ten Kevin wheels his chair back to 420, the keys in his fist, and on his way past the bed claps Jack once on the shoulder without a word. The tea lights along the sill start to die, one and then another, in no particular order.
At 11:58 by Theo’s laptop, Lena takes two deviled eggs off the milk glass, lays them in a paper napkin, and folds the corners in over them like a parish lady saving a plate for Father.
“Thank y’all for my funeral,” she says from the door. “The eggs were a corporal work of mercy.”
“Don’t you dare thank me,” says Laney, under the sunglasses. “Go.”
Jack walks her down.

s13b.slug: SATURDAY · 12:02 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — HER LANDING
body: They come down the two flights without a word, her a step ahead with her hand in her pocket on the napkin, his boots and her boots and nobody else in the well.

body.text: He knows this landing better by ear than by sight. On Tuesday night he sat two flights up and kept a decade a bead behind her by the click of the wood. He has never told her, and he doesn’t now.

body: The tube over her landing has a stammer in it tonight, a flicker every few seconds that no one has reported to anybody. The window in the door on two is black. Somewhere below, the last dryer in the laundry room is knocking a sneaker around, a slow dull thump that comes up the well and is the only sound in the building.
She doesn’t sit on her step. She stands on the landing with her back to the cinderblock and unfolds the napkin on her palm, one corner and then the next, and looks at her watch.
“Saturday,” she says, and holds one out to him.

Laney’s are Texas eggs, sweet relish in the yolk and a shake of paprika on top, and they have been sitting in a napkin in Lena’s coat pocket down two flights of stairs, and it’s the best thing he has eaten in a week. He eats it in two bites. Lena eats hers in four, carefully, with her other hand cupped under it for the paprika.
“Her mama’s,” she says, between the second bite and the third. “There’s an index card in a sandwich bag. It goes everywhere she goes, like a relic.”
When she’s done she licks a red smear off the side of her thumb, and he has to look at the stairs for a bit.

Four hours ago on the church steps they kissed, and it’s all over this landing. It’s in how she stands, with the cinderblock at her back and her chin up, and in how he has stopped one stair below her, the two of them set out like that without either one deciding it. He wants to kiss her again. Whatever that does to his face, it gets a corner of her mouth, and she looks down at the napkin.
She smooths the empty napkin flat against her palm and puts it in her pocket.
“You never asked me,” she says.
He waits.
“Not in all this time. And I know what it cost you not to, because I know what it would have cost me. We said we’d talk plain. So I’d rather you had it from me, on purpose, on a Saturday.”
She looks straight at him. “Never. Not with anyone.”
She doesn’t dress it up. She says it like the Mass times.
It’s the plainest thing anyone has ever said to him on a staircase, and he has been on a good many staircases this winter.
All fall and all of the winter there was a question he would not let into any room he was in, and it stood out in the hall of every one of them anyway, and it isn’t there now.
She waits for him with her hands in her coat pockets and her sentence already said.

body.text: On the levee, about Skye, he gave her *never that*. The rest of it is in his mouth.
On the levee he told her he had kept that. The rest of it is in his mouth.
His own answer is in his mouth.

choices.text: “Me either. Not with anyone.”
choices.key: On her landing after midnight, when Lena told you never, not with anyone, you told her the same: not with anyone.
response: “Me either,” he says. “Not with anyone.”
Out loud it sounds smaller than it has been all winter inside him. She takes it anyway. Her chin comes down, a little, as it does in a pew at the consecration, and comes back up.
“Goodnight, Youngstown,” she says.
He doesn’t move. For a second neither does she.

“You still haven’t asked me to dinner,” she says, and goes down the half flight to two with the napkin in her pocket. Through the wired glass in the door her shape goes off down the hall, cut into diamonds by the wire.

choices.text: “Not with anyone. I wanted you to hear it from me.”
choices.key: On her landing after midnight, when Lena told you never, not with anyone, you told her the same — and that you’d wanted her to hear it from you.
response: “Not with anyone,” he says. “I wanted you to hear it from me.”
“I heard it.” She says it like *amen* at the end of somebody else’s prayer: received, and that’s the end of the discussion.
She looks at his mouth. She takes her time about it. Then, deliberately, she looks at the door on two, like a woman at a counter checking the sign for what time they close.
“Dinner first,” she says, and steps down onto the half flight, and turns round on it with her hand on the rail.
“Goodnight, Jack.”

choices.text: “Not with anyone.” *And nothing else.*
choices.key: On her landing after midnight, when Lena told you never, not with anyone, you said it back — not with anyone — and nothing else.
response: “Not with anyone,” he says.

The quiet holds. Down in the laundry room the dryer gives up on the sneaker. She comes off the wall and up onto the first stair, close enough that he could count the freckles if he started, and then she doesn’t come any closer.
“Properly,” she says, like a password.
He goes up. Two flights, the rail cold under his hand, and at the turn he looks down the well, and she’s still on her landing with her hand in her coat pocket, on the napkin.

s14.slug: SATURDAY · 6:55 AM · THE ANCHOR — THE FISHERMEN
body: The sun isn’t over the mountains yet, and the harbor has the sky in it, blue-black going to pearl at the edges like the inside of a mussel shell. The boats that came in overnight are tied up below the Anchor’s windows with their decks hosed off and a gull on every rail.

body.text: Saturdays are Hector’s now. But Hector is at a christening in Oxnard, and Gloria called last night at ten, in the middle of a wake, and Jack said yes before she was done asking.
body.else: The fishermen shift is his, seven to one, the way it has been since he came back on the twentieth.

body: He got five hours. At five to seven he’s in the apron at the Hobart with the first rack of mugs going through, and at seven the fishermen come in out of the early cold in their rubber boots, and take the counter from Merle’s end stool in, and pay in cash, and the bell over the door doesn’t stop for twenty minutes.

On the shelf over the line Rudy’s radio is talking. No accordion this morning. A man’s voice, fast and serious, then a woman’s, then the man’s again, and through all of it Jack, whose Spanish is the Anchor’s Spanish — eggs, plates, hot, behind you, *mijo* — catches *Chile*, and *Chile* again, and a word he’s still working out when Rudy says it for him.
“*Terremoto*.” Rudy doesn’t turn it down. “Earthquake. In Chile. A big one, in the night.”

Over the sink, on the shelf where it lives, between the Ajax and a coffee can full of wooden spoons, Rudy’s rosary hangs on its nail, black beads and a tin cross. Rudy looks up at it once from the griddle, and back down at the eggs, and listens.

The fishermen know. Two of them heard it on the radio in their trucks on the way down. They talk about it the way they talk about weather, low and practical, with their elbows on the counter and their caps on: whether anything will come across. Whether it’ll be anything at all by the time it gets this far. One of them says his father took the boat out past the kelp once, the year of the Alaska one, to ride it out in deep water, and sat out there all night with the engine running, and nothing came. Another one says that’s how it goes, until it doesn’t. Before long they take their coffee to the front window and stand there in their boots with the mugs, looking at the harbor. The sun comes over the mountains while they stand there and catches the tops of the masts first, then the water, and the harbor lies flat and bright under it and tells them nothing either way.

Gloria crosses herself at the radio as she goes by under it, quick, with the coffeepot in her other hand. At the end stool Merle asks Rudy, in English, how many, and Rudy says nobody knows yet, and Merle nods at his eggs and leaves it there.
Jack runs the next rack. There’s nothing in his two hands to do about Chile but mugs, so he does mugs, and the Hobart roars and steams on its cycle, and the radio talks over it.

By nine the counter has emptied out, the fishermen gone back down the ramps to the boats with the radio still going in their trucks. Gloria comes along the counter with a rag and stops across from him where he’s racking clean mugs, and studies his face like the pie case at the start of a shift.
“Strawberry-rhubarb,” she says.
He waits for it.
“Something sour got in with something sweet,” Gloria says, “and now there’s no getting it back out. Sells, though.”
He racks the last of the mugs. On the radio the man is reading numbers now, slowly, and Rudy has gone very still at the griddle to hear them.
“Gloria,” Jack says. “Where does a man take a girl in this town, if he means to do it right?”
Gloria doesn’t ask who. She looks out the front window, past the fishermen’s trucks, down the length of the wharf.
“There’s a place at the end of the wharf with tablecloths,” she says. “They’ll want a jacket.”

response: “I have a jacket,” he says. “It says Carhartt on it.”
Gloria looks at the jacket on its hook by the back door, at the brown duck gone pale at the cuffs and the elbows, and back at him.
“Not that jacket.”

choices.text: “Thank you, Gloria.”
response: “Thank you, Gloria.”
She goes off down the counter without answering and comes back with a plate from the pass, two eggs over and a short stack and a side of bacon, and sets it on the steel in front of him instead.
“Eat.”

choices.text: “I don’t own a jacket.”
response: “I don’t own a jacket,” he says.
“Rudy’s got a wedding jacket.”
Rudy, at the line, doesn’t turn round from the radio. “Mijo. It’s brown.”
“Brown is a color,” Gloria says.

body: By one the wind has come round into the west and is knocking the tops off the swells out past the harbor mouth and standing the flags straight out on the wharf poles. He hangs up the apron. His hands come out of the last rack pink and pruned, gone soft and white at the fingertips from six hours of the Hobart, and he walks out the wharf instead of up it.
He wants to look at the place with the tablecloths from the outside, the way Frank looks a used truck over on the lot before he lets the man come out.

It’s most of the way to the end, past the fish market and the place that sells saltwater taffy, a long low building with more window than wall. Out past it there’s only the bait shack, and the end. At one in the afternoon there’s nobody eating. There are white tablecloths on every table, and the glasses upside down on them, and a man in a white jacket going between them with a cloth over his arm, polishing things that already shine. Jack stands outside in the wind with his pruned hands in the pockets of the Carhartt and looks at the tablecloths, and they look like a lot of money and three forks apiece.
Under the far end, the sea lions are barking on the crossbeams.

At the far end, at the rail, a girl in a watch cap is standing on an apple crate with a chrome movie camera up to her eye, her elbows in tight against the wind. Sol. And ten feet past her, at the rail, with nothing behind her but open water and the islands low and blue on the line of it, Skye.
She’s in a big cream sweater of her own with the sleeves pulled down over her hands, and her hair tied back in a scarf the wind keeps trying to take off her. She’s waving off a ship.

There is no ship. There’s the breakwater and the harbor mouth and a long way of bright, empty water. But she’s up on her toes at the rail with a white handkerchief, waving it big and slow over her head at somebody at another rail, going away. The handkerchief comes down to her mouth. It goes back up, smaller. She leans out after it over the water, farther than is safe, and catches herself with her other hand, and laughs up at the ship as if somebody at its rail has shouted a joke back across the water, and goes on waving long after there could be anybody out there left to see it.
A couple in matching windbreakers stops at the rail to watch her. The man says something, and the woman swats his arm, and they go on toward the taffy.

The Bolex doesn’t take sound. Whatever she wants it to have, she has to give it with her arms and her face and the wind. When the gusts drop he can hear the camera from where he stands, a small dry whir like a reel paying out line.
She’s good. From fifty yards off, with the wind taking every sound there is, he could tell you how far out the ship is.
He has stood at that rail at one in the morning with the RAZR hot against his ear and her voice coming up the coast from Studio City.
Sol lowers the camera.
Skye’s arm comes down. The handkerchief hangs from her fingers over the rail, and her face goes to nothing, and she turns it to the water and looks at the water a while.

Sol gets down off the crate and starts winding the Bolex with its little crank. Halfway through winding it she looks down the wharf, past the bait shack, and sees him. She looks at him for about as long as it takes to wind the spring the rest of the way. She goes on winding.
Skye’s face is to the water. She hasn’t looked up the wharf once.

choices.text: *Turn around before she can see you.*
choices.key: On the wharf you saw Skye at the rail, working a silent bit for Sol’s camera, and you turned around before she could see you.
response: He turns around before she can look up, and walks back the way he came, past the tablecloths and the taffy and the fish market, with the wind shoving at his back the length of the boards.
Behind him the sea lions are still at it under the far end.

choices.text: *Stand behind the bait shack till the bit is over. Then go.*
choices.key: On the wharf you watched Skye finish a silent bit for Sol’s camera from behind the bait shack, and then you went, and didn’t go to her.
response: He goes on as far as the bait shack and steps in behind it, out of the wind, where the lures hang on a pegboard in the window and a kid inside is counting frozen squid into a bag. From the corner of it he can see the rail.

Sol gets back up on her crate and raises the camera. Skye pushes the scarf off her forehead with the back of her wrist, and turns to the water, and starts it over from the beginning: up on her toes, the handkerchief, somebody at a rail going away from her.
He watches it all the way through this time, to the last wave, the small one, and goes while she’s still holding the handkerchief up to the water, to a ship that isn’t there.

choices.text: *Say her name once, too low for the wind to carry. Go.*
choices.key: On the wharf you saw Skye at the rail and said her name once, too low for anyone to hear, and didn’t go to her.
response: “Skye,” he says.
He says it once, low, a name said to somebody asleep. The wind comes straight down the wharf off the water and takes it back toward town, and none of it gets anywhere near the rail.
He goes. At the taffy place he looks back the once. She’s still looking at the water.

s16.slug: SATURDAY · 6:40 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — TWO INVITATIONS
body: The last of Saturday is going out of the top of the window in 412, a band of apricot over the ridge with the eucalyptus standing up black in front of it. Jack has been back long enough to shower and not long enough to get the Anchor’s fryer out from under his nails. He’s at his desk with *The Moviegoer* shut in front of him. Since the wharf a picture has been coming back to him every few minutes, a rail and a camera and a face, and every time it comes he lets it, and lets it go back where it came from.

Theo is on his bed in a T-shirt and his good trousers, the MacBook open on his knees and three DVD cases fanned out on the blanket beside him like a hand he’s deciding how to play. He picks one and holds it up by the corner.
“*The Apartment*. Nineteen-sixty. Wilder. You’ve never seen it, which is a moral failing. I’ve been waiting all week with nothing on it.”
“How do you know I’ve never seen it?”
“Because you’ve never brought it up. People who’ve seen it bring it up.”
The RAZR goes off on the desk by his elbow, and the outside screen lights with her name.

s16l.slug: SATURDAY · 7:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE PARISH KITCHEN — NOT A DATE
body: The parish kitchen is three steps down at the back of the hall, a long room in stainless steel and church-basement green, with a six-burner range older than anyone who cooks on it and a window over the sinks that looks out on the courtyard. Father Osei’s office is on the other side of the wall, and through it, turned low, comes a highlife record, horns going round over a guitar.

Lena is at the range in a bib apron that says ST. BRENDAN ALTAR SOCIETY and comes nearly to her shins, her sleeves shoved up past the elbow and her hair tied back with the twist tie off a bread bag. On the burner is the biggest Dutch oven the parish owns. On the board beside it sit four yellow onions, a head of celery, three green peppers, and a knife laid across them like a place setting.
“This isn’t a date,” she says. “Dates have reservations. This is a vegetable.” She holds out an onion.
He takes it. It’s cold from the walk-in, and the skin comes away like tissue paper in his palm.
“Onion, celery, bell pepper,” Lena says. “The trinity. Couldn’t a soul tell you exactly what the celery does, and you’d know in a heartbeat if it wasn’t there. So you be respectful with the celery.”

He is respectful with the celery. He chops the way Rudy showed him on slow nights at the Anchor, fingertips curled back out of the blade’s way and the knife doing the work, and she watches the first onion go into a neat white heap, and makes a small approving noise, and turns back to her pot.

The oil is in already. She shakes the flour over it out of a Folgers can and starts in with a wooden spoon whose end has gone black from forty years of exactly this, and the kitchen fills up with it toasting, warm, part bakery and part struck match. It’s for the Newman supper after the five o’clock tomorrow, chicken and andouille for forty, the stock already going on the back burner. “It’s Sunday tomorrow,” she says, “and on a Sunday the Church permits a girl a sausage, and I intend to be permitted.”
When the onions are done she hands him the spoon. “The color of a penny,” she says, “then a Hershey bar, then you stop or you start over. That’s Daddy’s. Don’t you walk away from it.”

He knows better than to walk away from it. He stirs, and she takes the knife and does the peppers, fast, and then the celery, with exaggerated reverence. The board is at his elbow. When she reaches past him for the bowl her forearm goes along his, flour on hers and onion on his, and comes back. She leans her hip on the counter beside the range, near enough that he can feel the warmth of her through his shirtsleeve, and watches the roux go from blond toward peanut butter under the spoon.

In the window over the sinks the moon has come up full behind the olive tree, and the courtyard is silver and black: the folding tables stacked against the wall for tomorrow, and the old brass sprinkler head, a knob in the flower bed, behaving itself.

Halfway to peanut butter, Father Osei comes past the kitchen door in his black clerical shirt with the sleeves rolled. He takes a spoon from the drawer by the door, dips it in the stockpot, tastes, drops the spoon in the sink, and goes back out the way he came. The horns through the wall go on.

It’s a long stir. Forty-five minutes, or as long as it takes. He has her at his elbow for every one of them, the soap in her hair and the onion on her fingers, her voice going on about the Newman treasurer and a casserole dish nobody has seen since Ash Wednesday, the pot under his spoon going darker by degrees. There’s flour on the inside of her wrist. She told him in the doorway what this is, and it’s a vegetable.

choices.text: “Tell me about your father’s.”
choices.key: In the parish kitchen on Saturday night you asked Lena about her father’s roux, and she told you while you stirred.
response: “Tell me about your father’s.”

She watches the spoon go round before she answers. “Sundays,” she says. “After the ten-thirty, with the house full of everybody. He’d have the stove, and he’d open a Dixie and set it on the back corner, and never drink it. Every Sunday. That beer just sat there getting warm. I asked him one time what it was for, and he said it was for his hands, so they’d have somewhere to be that wasn’t the spoon.” She pushes a piece of hair off her face with the back of her wrist. “He said a roux will tell you when. You just have to be standing there when it does.”
Then she reaches over and takes the spoon out of his hand without a word. It’s time; he can see it in the pot, dark as the chocolate bar, and she’s the one standing there.

choices.text: “It’s the color of a penny. Do I stop or start over?”
choices.key: In the parish kitchen on Saturday night you asked Lena whether a penny-colored roux meant stop or start over.
response: “It’s the color of a penny,” he says. “Do I stop or start over?”
“Keep going, Youngstown. Nobody stops at a penny.”

Her hand comes over his on the spoon, flour-dry and warm, and takes the pot round with it, one slow turn, scraping the corners he’s been missing, and then it’s back on the cutting board, busy with the celery, as though it had never been anywhere else.

choices.text: *Keep stirring. Don’t look at her.*
choices.key: In the parish kitchen on Saturday night you kept stirring Lena’s roux and didn’t look at her, with her right there at your elbow.
response: He keeps stirring. He keeps his eyes on the pot.

She’s right there at his elbow. He can feel her looking at the side of his face, and she goes on looking long enough for the roux to go a shade darker under it, and he gives the pot everything he has: the corners, the bottom, the slow brown coming round and round.
“It’s done,” she says, and takes the spoon.

s16t.slug: SATURDAY · 7:00 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — THE APARTMENT
body: Theo’s rule is that you don’t watch black and white with a lamp on. “It’s like reading Dickens in a dentist’s office.” So the lamp is off, and the MacBook sits on its pillow on the desk chair between the beds, the brightest thing in 412, and the two of them lie on their own beds on their sides with their heads propped on their hands, too old for a sleepover by a couple of years and not caring.
In the window the moon has come up full over the ridge, so white it could have walked out of the picture.

It opens in an insurance company in New York, a floor of desks going back so far they stop being desks and turn into a pattern, and at one of them, with an adding machine and a cold coming on, Jack Lemmon. Lemmon has an apartment. Men above him at the company borrow the key, so they’ll have somewhere to take women who aren’t their wives, and they pay him in promises about promotions, and he stands out on the sidewalk in the cold waiting for them to be finished with his own bed. Shirley MacLaine runs one of the elevators. By her second ride Jack can see how this is going to go for Lemmon, and so can Lemmon, and knowing doesn’t do either of them any good. When Lemmon buys a bowler hat to go with his promotion and tries it on for her in the elevator, Jack is so far on his side it hurts.

Theo has seen it, by his own count, forty times. He watches maybe one scene in three. The rest of the time, when Jack glances across the desk chair, Theo is watching him, the screen light on half his face, the way a man drives a friend through the town he grew up in and watches the friend instead of the town. He comes in a hair behind Jack on every joke, checking it still works on somebody new. Now and then he says something into the dark, never over a line, always in the gaps: “Watch his hands. Lemmon acts with his hands better than most people act with their faces.” And later, as the elevator doors close on MacLaine: “Wilder never lets her be the joke. Notice that. Everybody else in the building is a joke.” There’s a bowl of kettle corn from the Mesa farmers’ market on the desk chair beside the laptop, and every so often one of them reaches over in the dark and the other one hears it. When Lemmon drains a pot of spaghetti through a tennis racket, Jack laughs so hard and so suddenly that he has to sit up, and across the room Theo puts his face in his pillow and comes up out of it with his hair wrecked.
It isn’t only funny. Past the middle it goes somewhere dark that Jack didn’t see coming, and for that stretch Theo watches the screen and not him.

By the end it’s New Year’s Eve. MacLaine has heard something at a party that makes her put down her glass and leave, and she’s running down a New York street in her good coat with the noisemakers going behind her, and Jack is up on one elbow.
“I’m happy for you,” Theo says. He says it to the screen, with the girl in the coat running on it. “I’m going to be happy on a delay.”
His eyes stay on her.

choices.text: “Take the delay. I’ll wait.”
choices.key: Watching *The Apartment* in the dark, when Theo said he was happy for you on a delay, you told him to take the delay — you’d wait.
response: “Take the delay,” Jack says. “I’ll wait.”
Theo nods, at the screen. “Okay.”

choices.text: “Picture it. A man. A laptop. A delay.”
choices.key: Watching *The Apartment* in the dark, when Theo said he was happy for you on a delay, you handed him back one of his own loglines.
response: “Picture it,” Jack says. “A man. A laptop. A delay.”
Theo laughs, caught. “Derivative.”
On the screen MacLaine gets where she’s going. Theo watches her get there, and lays his head back down on his arm. “You’ll owe me a kidney for that.”

choices.text: *Say nothing. Watch the end with him.*
choices.key: Watching *The Apartment* in the dark, when Theo said he was happy for you on a delay, you said nothing and watched the end with him.
response: Jack lies back down on his arm. They watch the end of it together, two beds and a desk chair and a picture fifty years old, with nothing said.
The credits come up. Theo rolls onto his back and tells the ceiling, quietly, “Best Picture. Nineteen sixty,” like a prayer he has known since he was small.

s17.slug: SUNDAY · 11:30 AM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE TRANSFIGURATION
body: The 11:30 is St. Brendan’s at its fullest: families from the Mesa in the front half with their children graded by height, a rank of students in the back still damp from the shower, the Coffee & Donuts ladies on the aisle ends where they can get out quick. The sun is high enough now to come through the blue glass from outside, and it lays its color down the fir ribs and across the tile. The flower stands are empty. The purple is on the ambo and the altar cloth and, in a minute, on Father Osei.
Jack takes a pew on the Mary side, about halfway up, the aisle end, and kneels. He is partway into a Hail Mary when the kneeler takes somebody’s weight beside him.

It’s Lena, in the long coat, with the lace folded in her hand. She kneels, and crosses herself, and is quiet a little with her eyes shut. Then she sits back, and shakes the lace out, and puts it on her hair.

body.text: Settling her coat, she leans to him under the organ’s first chords and informs him that he still smells like her onions.
Settling her coat, she leans to him under the organ’s first chords and asks him how the movie was. He tells her Theo says it was a moral failing he’d never seen it. “It was,” she says.

body: Gus Ferreira brings them to their feet with the entrance hymn, a Lenten one, each line of it coming down a step lower at the end than it started. Father Osei comes up the aisle in the purple behind the cross. Where the Gloria would go there is only the sound of a full church sitting down.

A man from the Mesa in a sport coat reads Genesis: Abram brought outside in the dark and told to look up and count the stars, if he can; and then the strange part, the animals cut in two and laid out in the night, and a smoking pot and a flaming torch passing between the halves on their own. Jack has always liked that part. Abram is asleep through it. The fire keeps both ends of the bargain by itself.

Kenzie Rourke from Newman cantors the psalm, *The Lord is my light and my salvation*, and the church gives it back to her, and beside him Lena’s voice comes in under the line and stays on the last note a hair after everybody else has let it go.

There’s no Alleluia before the Gospel. Gus plays the Lenten acclamation instead, and they stand, and Father Osei reads Luke. Peter and James and John taken up the mountain to pray, and while he prays the Lord’s face changes and his clothes go dazzling white, and Moses and Elijah are there talking with him about what is going to happen to him in Jerusalem. Peter has been asleep. He wakes and sees them, and says, “Master, it is good that we are here,” and offers to put up three tents, one apiece, not knowing what he’s saying. And then the cloud comes down over all of them, and they’re afraid inside it, and the voice: *This is my chosen Son; listen to him.* When it lifts, there is only Jesus. And they fell silent, Father Osei reads, and did not at that time tell anyone what they had seen.

He comes down to the sanctuary step for the homily and stands there with his hands folded. “Peter wants to build a house for the glory and live in it,” he says. “The Lord lets them see it once, so that they can carry it down the mountain into Jerusalem, where they will need it.” He goes back to his chair. In the pew behind them somebody approves of the length with a single “Mm.”

In the prayers of the faithful the man in the sport coat reads one for Chile: for the dead and the injured, for those who have lost their homes, and for everyone still waiting for news. *Lord, hear our prayer.* Lena’s fingers have been turning down the corner of her missalette. At *Chile* they stop. Her hands go still on the back of the pew in front of them and lie there, through the response and the petition after it, the hands of a girl from a coast. Jack keeps his eyes on the altar. At the Amen her hands come back to her.

The bells at the consecration, and a hundred kneelers coming down at once like a strike on league night in Boardman. St. Brendan’s doesn’t hold hands at the Our Father. Lena folds hers. His hang at his sides. Her voice goes along at his shoulder, low, a half-word ahead of his the length of the prayer, and they come to *deliver us from evil* together, and Father Osei goes on alone.

He wishes them the peace of the Lord, and the church tells him *and also with you*, and he asks them to offer one another a sign of peace. All around them hands go out across the pews. Lena turns to him first. She holds out her hand and he takes it: warm from being folded, a nick across one knuckle from a paring knife, a grip like a handshake on a deal for about as long as it takes him to notice, and then not like a handshake at all.

choices.text: *Say it the way it’s said.* “Peace be with you.”
response: “Peace be with you.”
“And also with you.”
When it’s time they go up to Communion together. In the line she’s in front of him, and the lace has slipped crooked over one ear, and he looks at it the length of the aisle and doesn’t fix it.

choices.text: “Peace be with you, Lena.”
response: “Peace be with you, Lena.”
Her name, in the middle of the church. Her hand tightens on his. “And also with you, Jack.”

choices.text: *Say it, and let go first.*
response: “Peace be with you.”
“And also with you.”
He lets go first. She notices; a small line comes between her brows and goes. Later, going up the aisle to Communion, her knuckles find his, going by, and are gone again.

s17a.slug: SUNDAY · 12:40 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD — COFFEE & DONUTS
body: Coffee & Donuts happens in the courtyard after the 11:30 in any weather, and today the weather has come round to it: the fog burned off by noon and the sun coming down through the olive tree onto three folding tables, two urns, a sleeve of styrofoam cups and four pink boxes going fast. Father Osei’s office window is open over the courtyard, and inside it his record player is going at a volume the Coffee & Donuts ladies gave up complaining about years ago, a dance band from Accra, horns out front and a guitar picking along underneath like somebody walking quickly to a party he’s glad to be asked to. Father Osei himself is down here at the urn in his black shirt, pouring, and the record plays on up there without him.

Sunday isn’t a fast day. Lena eats a glazed donut standing at the end of the table, with the unhurried devotion of a woman who had bread and water on Friday and hasn’t forgotten it, and goes back for another. Jack has one in a napkin and forgets it’s there.
“He’s right about Peter,” she says, with her mouth full, nodding up at the open window. “Peter is a man who’d build you a carport while you were trying to tell him something.”
“I like Peter.”

“Everybody likes Peter. Peter is who you want at a crawfish boil. You would not put Peter in charge of the tents.” She looks at the last bite of the donut, and takes it. “I dreamed about a po’boy Friday night. Shrimp. Dressed. I woke up and said a whole Act of Contrition over a sandwich I never ate.”
“Did it take?”
“It’s Sunday. I’m eating the evidence.”

The first of Lena’s three instructions is his to carry out. He has had since Friday night to get it right, in the shower and again in the Communion line, and it has gone out of his head like a homily on the drive home. He puts the donut down on the end of the table. His hands are steadier than they were on Wednesday. They aren’t steady.
“Lena,” he says. “I wanted to ask you — ”

Under the flower bed, a valve that has been in the ground since 1962 makes up its mind. The brass head comes up hissing sideways, spits at the bench, and then finds its arc and lets fly: a long fan of water that comes round across the flower bed, across the end of the first table, across the pink boxes and the two of them, and keeps on coming.

The courtyard scatters. The Coffee & Donuts ladies snatch the pink boxes to their chests. A man in a Giants cap holds his cup over his head and gets soaked anyway. A little girl in patent-leather shoes runs straight into it, shrieking, and has to be retrieved. Mrs. Fitch walks out of range at precisely her ordinary pace, coffee aloft. Jack and Lena run the other way, for the olive tree, and get in under it with water rattling in the leaves over their heads and Lena laughing so hard she has to put a hand on the trunk. “Sweet suffering Saint Sebastian,” she says, when she can, to the general situation. Out by the tables one of the Coffee & Donuts ladies, rescuing the creamer, looks over at the two of them under the tree, and then looks very hard at the creamer.
She has saved his donut. Her lace is wet and one side of her coat is wet, and the donut, held high the entire time, is perfect.

Father Osei comes over from the urn, which the sprinkler doesn’t reach and never has, with a stack of paper napkins. He gives one to Lena and one to Jack. “It does this,” he says. “It has done this since before I came. Dry your hands. There are more glazed.” He goes back to the urn and pours for the man in the Giants cap, who has decided to find it funny.

Under the olive tree, with the water swinging round on the far side of the trunk and the leaves still dripping on them, Lena dries her face with the napkin and looks up at him, wet to the hairline, and waits.
“You were saying.”

s18.slug: SUNDAY · 6:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — THE BROWNS
body: The afternoon went to the hockey final: the fourth-floor lounge full to the doors by the third period, and in overtime, when the puck went in and it was over, a girl in a red Team Canada sweater standing on the couch with both arms up, screaming, and Jack in the doorway thinking of Kyle peeling off a jersey in a bar in Burnaby and Gord with the mustache rising off his stool, and of the girl who told him about them in lowercase, and smiling at a room full of strangers who thought it was about the hockey.

Now the lounge is a drift of popcorn and the stairwell is his. He’s on his step. The RAZR goes at six-thirty exactly; Ma has never been late for anything in her life and isn’t going to start on account of the Olympics.

body.text: “Did you ask Lena?”
“It was Friday,” Ma says. “Did you ask her?”
“Is it still ‘not yet’?”
“To dinner.”
body.else: “No, Ma. I asked her. To dinner.”

body: “*Good.*”
He hears the dish towel go down on the counter. She has stopped whatever she was doing to hear the rest of it, and there isn’t much rest yet, and she takes what there is.
“Did you eat?”
“A donut.”
“A donut is not eating,” Ma says. “A donut is what you have while you decide what to eat. Where are you taking her?”
“Someplace with tablecloths.”
“Then iron something.”
“I’ll iron something, Ma.”
Behind her, from the door to the garage, at full volume: “ASK HIM DOES SHE LIKE THE BROWNS.”
“Your father wants to know — ”
“I heard him, Ma.”
“The street heard him.”
“Tell him she’s a Saints fan.”

Ma, away from the phone: “She’s a Saints fan, Frank.” Out in the garage a silence follows, the length of a man revising a lifetime of opinions about Louisiana. Then, at the same volume: “TELL HER CONGRATULATIONS.”
“She knows more football than he does,” Jack says.
“I’m not telling him that. He’s got the hood up.”

She tells him the rest of the week on Glenwood Avenue: the furnace man, Rosie’s cough, a snow on Thursday that’s still in the gutters going black. Then, when the garage has been quiet a while: “Your grandmother lit her candle. After the nine o’clock. She sat with it till the ten-thirty people came in and made her move.”
“Tell her thank you.”
“She knows.”

Out in the garage the compressor kicks on, and his father hollers something about a light, and Ma says, “I’m on with your son,” and then, to Jack, “He wants me to hold the light,” and goes to hold it. The stairwell is quiet. It’s ten past seven.
